title.zh: 卷十九 魏書十九 任城陳蕭王傳
title.en: Volume 19: Book of Wei 19 - Biographies of the princes of Rencheng, Chen, and Xiao
title.raw: 卷十九 魏書十九 任城陳蕭王傳 Volume 19: Book of Wei 19 - Biographies of the princes of Rencheng, Chen, and Xiao

sentences.zh: 任城王曹彰 陳思王曹植 蕭懷王曹熊

translations.literal: The Prince of Rencheng, Cao Zhang; the Prince of Chensi, Cao Zhi; the Prince of Xiaohuai, Cao Xiong.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhang, Prince of Rencheng; Cao Zhi, Prince of Chensi; and Cao Xiong, Prince of Xiaohuai.

sentences.zh: 任城王曹彰

translations.literal: The Prince of Rencheng, Cao Zhang.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhang, Prince of Rencheng.

sentences.zh: 任城威王彰，字子文。

translations.literal: Cao Zhang, posthumous name Wei, Prince of Rencheng, had the courtesy name Ziwen.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhang, posthumously known as Prince Wei of Rencheng, bore the courtesy name Ziwen.

sentences.zh: 少善射御，膂力過人，手格猛獸，不避險阻。

translations.literal: In youth he was skilled at archery and riding; his bodily strength surpassed others; with his hands he grappled fierce beasts; he did not avoid perilous obstacles.
translations.idiomatic: From boyhood he excelled at archery and horsemanship, possessed uncanny strength, wrestled dangerous beasts bare-handed, and never shrank from rough ground.

sentences.zh: 數從征伐，志意慷慨。

translations.literal: Repeatedly he followed on campaigns; his resolve and intent were ardent and bold.
translations.idiomatic: He rode again and again on campaign, fired by an ardent, martial spirit.

sentences.zh: 太祖嘗抑之曰：『汝不念讀書慕聖道，而好乘汗馬擊劍，此一夫之用，何足貴也！

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor once restrained him, saying, "You do not think of reading books and yearning for the sages' Way, but delight in mounting sweat-drenched horses and wielding the sword—this is the use of a single fellow; what is there to esteem in it!"
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao once tried to check him: "You give no thought to study or the path of the sages, yet you love galloping horses and crossing swords. Any brawler can do that—why should it be prized?"

sentences.zh: 』課彰讀《詩》、《書》，彰謂左右曰：『丈夫一為衛、霍，將十萬騎馳沙漠，驅戎狄，立功建號耳，何能作博士邪？

translations.literal: He assigned Zhang to read the Shijing and Shujing. Zhang said to those about him, "A real man ought once to become a Wei Qing or Huo Qubing, leading a hundred thousand riders racing through the desert, driving off the Rong and Di, and establishing merit and a resounding name—how could he become a Doctor of Classics?"
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao set him lessons in the Odes and Documents, but Zhang told his attendants, "A man worth the name should ride at the head of a hundred thousand like Wei Qing or Huo Qubing—sweep the deserts, scatter the barbarians, and win a general's fame. What would I do with a scholar's cap?"

sentences.zh: 』太祖嘗問諸子所好，使各言其志。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor once asked his various sons what they delighted in and had each state his ambition.
translations.idiomatic: Once Cao Cao asked each of his sons what he enjoyed and had them speak his mind.

sentences.zh: 彰曰：『好為將。

translations.literal: Zhang said, "I delight in being a general."
translations.idiomatic: Zhang replied: "I want to command armies."

sentences.zh: 』太祖曰：『為將柰何？

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor said, "Being a general—how is that done?"
translations.idiomatic: "What does a general do?" asked Cao Cao.

sentences.zh: 』對曰：『被堅執銳，臨難不顧，為士卒先；

translations.literal: He replied, "Donning hard armor and grasping sharp weapons, facing danger without flinching, going ahead of the soldiers;"
translations.idiomatic: "Clad in armor, spear in hand," he answered, "I would meet peril head-on and lead from the front,"

sentences.zh: 賞必行，罰必信。

translations.literal: rewards must be carried out; punishments must be trustworthy."
translations.idiomatic: "with rewards kept when promised and punishments given without fail."

sentences.zh: 』太祖大笑。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor laughed greatly.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao roared with laughter.

sentences.zh: 建安二十一年，封鄢陵侯。

translations.literal: In the twenty-first year of Jian'an, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yanling.
translations.idiomatic: In 216 he was made Marquis of Yanling.

sentences.zh: 二十三年，代郡烏丸反，以彰為北中郎將，行驍騎將軍。

translations.literal: In the twenty-third year, the Wuhuan of Dai commandery rebelled; Zhang was made General of the Household for the North and acting General of Swift Cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: In 218 the Wuhuan of Dai rose; Cao Zhang was appointed General of the Household for the North and acting General of Swift Cavalry to deal with them.

sentences.zh: 臨發，太祖戒彰曰：『居家為父子，受事為君臣，動以王法從事，爾其戒之！

translations.literal: As he was about to depart, the Grand Progenitor admonished Zhang, saying, "At home we are father and son; when receiving tasks we are lord and minister; in action follow the king's law—be mindful of this!"
translations.idiomatic: On the eve of his departure Cao Cao warned him: "Under this roof we are father and son; on duty we are sovereign and subject. Act only as the law allows—remember that."

sentences.zh: 』彰北征，入涿郡界，叛胡數千騎卒至。

translations.literal: Zhang campaigned north, entered the borders of Zhuo commandery, and several thousand rebel Hu horsemen suddenly arrived.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang marched north into Zhuo, where several thousand rebel horsemen fell on him without warning.

sentences.zh: 時兵馬未集，唯有步卒千人，騎數百匹。

translations.literal: At that time troops and horses had not yet assembled; there were only a thousand foot soldiers and several hundred mounts.
translations.idiomatic: His main force had not yet come up; he had only a thousand foot soldiers and a few hundred horses.

sentences.zh: 用田豫計，固守要隙，虜乃退散。

translations.literal: Employing Tian Yu's plan, he firmly defended critical defiles, and the raiders then withdrew and scattered.
translations.idiomatic: Following Tian Yu's advice, he held the key passes until the enemy broke and withdrew.

sentences.zh: 彰追之，身自搏戰，射胡騎，應弦而倒者前後相屬。

translations.literal: Zhang pursued them, personally joining battle, shooting Hu riders; those who fell at the twang of the bowstring followed one after another.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang gave chase, fighting in the thick of it himself; his bowstring sang and Hu horsemen tumbled from their saddles in an unbroken line.

sentences.zh: 戰過半日，彰鎧中數箭，意氣益厲，乘勝逐北，至于桑乾，

translations.literal: The fighting passed half a day; Zhang's armor took several arrows; his spirit grew fiercer; riding victory he pursued the fleeing enemy as far as Sanggan,
translations.idiomatic: After half a day of fighting, his armor studded with arrows, he only fought harder; he pressed the rout all the way to the Sanggan River,

sentences.zh: 〈臣松之案桑乾縣屬代郡，今北虜居之，號為索干之都。〉

translations.literal: 〈Your subject Pei Songzhi notes: Sanggan county belonged to Dai commandery; now the northern barbarians dwell there and style it the capital of Suogan.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈Pei Songzhi remarks that Sanggan County lay in Dai; northern peoples now hold the place and call it the "Suogan" capital.〉

sentences.zh: 去代二百餘里。

translations.literal: It was more than two hundred li from Dai.
translations.idiomatic: more than two hundred li beyond the seat of Dai.

sentences.zh: 長史諸將皆以為新涉遠，士馬疲頓，又受節度，不得過代，不可深進，違令輕敵。

translations.literal: The chief clerk and the various generals all held that they had newly crossed far ground, men and horses were weary and exhausted, and moreover they were under orders of control, not permitted to cross Dai; they could not advance deeply; to violate orders and treat the enemy lightly.
translations.idiomatic: His chief of staff and commanders argued that the army was worn from a long march, bound by orders not to cross beyond Dai, and that to push farther would mean disobeying orders and underestimating the foe.

sentences.zh: 彰曰：『率師而行，唯利所在，何節度乎？

translations.literal: Zhang said, "Leading an army on the march, wherever profit lies—what is there to orders of control?"
translations.idiomatic: Zhang retorted: "An army on the march goes where victory lies—what do written orders matter?"

sentences.zh: 胡走未遠，追之必破。

translations.literal: The Hu have not fled far; pursuing them will surely break them.
translations.idiomatic: The Hu are still within reach; a hard pursuit will shatter them.

sentences.zh: 從令縱敵，非良將也。

translations.literal: Obeying orders and letting the enemy go is not the mark of a good general."
translations.idiomatic: To obey a slip of paper and let the enemy escape is no way for a real commander.

sentences.zh: 』遂上馬，令軍中：『後出者斬。

translations.literal: Thereupon he mounted his horse and ordered the army: "Whoever comes out last shall be beheaded."
translations.idiomatic: He swung into the saddle and told the ranks: "The last man out of the fight dies."

sentences.zh: 』一日一夜與虜相及，擊，大破之，斬首獲生以千數。

translations.literal: In one day and one night he caught up with the raiders, struck them, and greatly shattered them; heads taken and captives numbered in the thousands.
translations.idiomatic: In a day and a night he overtook them, smashed their host, and counted beheads and prisoners by the thousand.

sentences.zh: 彰乃倍常科大賜將士，將士無不悅喜。

translations.literal: Zhang then doubled the usual scale of rewards and greatly bestowed on officers and soldiers; the officers and soldiers were without exception pleased and joyful.
translations.idiomatic: He doubled the usual bounty for the troops, and every man in the ranks went home delighted.

sentences.zh: 時鮮卑大人軻比能將數萬騎觀望彊 弱，見彰力戰，所向皆破，乃請服。

translations.literal: At that time the Xianbei chieftain Kebineng led several tens of thousands of riders watching the relative strength and weakness; seeing Zhang fight with force, wherever he turned all was broken, and thereupon he requested submission.
translations.idiomatic: Kebineng, chief of the Xianbei, had brought tens of thousands of horsemen to watch how the fight went; when he saw Zhang tear through every line before him, he offered his surrender.

sentences.zh: 北方悉平。

translations.literal: The north was entirely pacified.
translations.idiomatic: The northern frontier was quiet at last.

sentences.zh: 時太祖在長安，召彰詣行在所。

translations.literal: At that time the Grand Progenitor was at Chang'an and summoned Zhang to the imperial headquarters.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao was then at Chang'an and ordered Zhang to report to court.

sentences.zh: 彰自代過鄴，太子謂彰曰：『卿新有功，今西見上，宜勿自伐，應對常若不足者。

translations.literal: Zhang passed from Dai through Ye; the Heir Apparent said to Zhang, "You have newly achieved merit; now going west to see the Sovereign, you ought not to boast of yourself; in answering always be as if insufficient."
translations.idiomatic: Passing through Ye from Dai, the heir Cao Pi told him: "You have fresh laurels; when you see our father in the west, do not preen. Speak as though your deeds were never enough."

sentences.zh: 』彰到，如太子言，歸功諸將。

translations.literal: When Zhang arrived, as the Heir Apparent had said, he attributed merit to the various generals.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang did exactly that: before Cao Cao he laid the credit at his generals' feet.

sentences.zh: 太祖喜，持彰鬚曰：『黃鬚兒竟大奇也！』

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor was pleased, grasped Zhang's beard, and said, "The yellow-bearded boy is indeed greatly extraordinary!"
translations.idiomatic: Delighted, Cao Cao tugged at his whiskers and cried, "My yellow-bearded son—you are a wonder!"

sentences.zh: 〈魏略曰：太祖在漢中，而劉備栖於山頭，使劉封下挑戰。

translations.literal: 〈The Weilüe states: The Grand Progenitor was in Hanzhong, while Liu Bei lodged on a hilltop and sent Liu Feng down to challenge to battle.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Weilüe records that while Cao Cao was in Hanzhong, Liu Bei camped on a height and sent Liu Feng down to taunt him.〉

sentences.zh: 太祖罵曰：『賣履舍兒，長使假子拒汝公乎！

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor cursed, saying, "Shoemaker's brat, do you always send a false son to resist your lord father!"
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao swore: "You sandal-seller's whelp—do you mean to fend off your elder with a borrowed son?"

sentences.zh: 待呼我黃鬚來，令擊之。

translations.literal: Wait until I call my yellow-bearded one and have him strike them.
translations.idiomatic: Wait till I fetch my yellow-beard and set him on you."

sentences.zh: 』乃召彰。

translations.literal: Thereupon he summoned Zhang.
translations.idiomatic: He then sent for Cao Zhang.

sentences.zh: 彰晨夜進道，西到長安而太祖已還，從漢中而歸。

translations.literal: Zhang pressed the road day and night; arriving west at Chang'an, the Grand Progenitor had already returned, coming back from Hanzhong.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang raced night and day to Chang'an, but Cao Cao had already quit Hanzhong and was on his way home.

sentences.zh: 彰鬚黃，故以呼之。〉

translations.literal: Zhang's whiskers were yellow; therefore he was called by this.〉
translations.idiomatic: Zhang's beard was yellow, which earned him the nickname.〉

sentences.zh: 太祖東還，以彰行越騎將軍，留長安。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor returned east and, with Zhang acting as General Who Crosses the River on Horseback, left him at Chang'an.
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Cao marched east again, he named Zhang acting General Who Crosses the River on Horseback and left him to hold Chang'an.

sentences.zh: 太祖至洛陽，得疾，驛召彰，未至，太祖崩。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor reached Luoyang, fell ill, and by post-station summons called Zhang; before he arrived, the Grand Progenitor passed away.
translations.idiomatic: Taken ill at Luoyang, Cao Cao urgently summoned Zhang; before Zhang could arrive, he died.

sentences.zh: 〈魏略曰：彰至，謂臨菑侯植曰：『先王召我者，欲立汝也。

translations.literal: 〈The Weilüe states: When Zhang arrived, he said to Marquis of Linzi Zhi, "The late king summoned me because he wished to establish you."〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Weilüe says that when Zhang reached Luoyang he told Cao Zhi, Marquis of Linzi: "Father called for me because he meant to make you heir."〉

sentences.zh: 』植曰：『不可。

translations.literal: Zhi said, "It cannot be done."
translations.idiomatic: Zhi answered: "That must not be."

sentences.zh: 不見袁氏兄弟乎！』〉

translations.literal: Have you not seen the Yuan brothers!"〉
translations.idiomatic: Have you forgotten what became of the Yuan brothers?"〉

sentences.zh: 文帝即王位，彰與諸侯就國。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wen assumed the kingly throne, Zhang together with the various feudal lords proceeded to their states.
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Pi took the title of King of Wei, Zhang and the other enfeoffed princes went out to their fiefs.

sentences.zh: 〈魏略曰：太子嗣立，既葬，遣彰之國。

translations.literal: 〈The Weilüe states: When the Heir Apparent succeeded to the position, after the burial, he sent Zhang to his state.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Weilüe says that once the heir had succeeded and the late king was buried, he sent Zhang off to his fief.〉

sentences.zh: 始彰自以先王見任有功，冀因此遂見授用，而聞當隨例，意甚不悅，不待遣而去。

translations.literal: At first Zhang, because the late king had employed him in view of merit, hoped thereby to be seen and appointed to use; but hearing that he was to follow precedent, his intent was greatly displeased, and without awaiting dispatch he departed.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang had hoped his father's trust and battlefield record would win him a post at court; learning he was to be packed off like any other prince, he left in a sulk before the formal order came.

sentences.zh: 時以鄢陵塉薄，使治中牟。

translations.literal: At that time because Yanling was barren and thin, he was made to administer Zhongmou.
translations.idiomatic: Because his Yanling fief was poor soil, he was reassigned to govern from Zhongmou.

sentences.zh: 及帝受禪，因封為中牟王。

translations.literal: When the Emperor received the abdication, thereupon he was enfeoffed as King of Zhongmou.
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Pi took the throne, Zhang was raised to King of Zhongmou.

sentences.zh: 是後大駕幸許昌，北州諸侯上下，皆畏彰之剛嚴；

translations.literal: After this, when the great chariot visited Xuchang, the feudal lords of the northern provinces above and below all feared Zhang's stern rigor;
translations.idiomatic: Thereafter, whenever the court moved to Xuchang, the northern princes high and low went in awe of Zhang's iron discipline;

sentences.zh: 每過中牟，不敢不速。〉

translations.literal: whenever passing Zhongmou, they did not dare not be swift.〉
translations.idiomatic: and none dared loiter when his route took him past Zhongmou.〉

sentences.zh: 詔曰：『先王之道，庸勳親親，並建母弟，開國承家，故能藩屏大宗，禦侮厭難。

translations.literal: An edict stated, "The Way of the former kings: employing merit and cherishing kin, together establishing mothers' younger brothers, opening states and inheriting houses—thereby they were able to screen and shield the great lineage, resist insult, and quell hardship."
translations.idiomatic: An edict declared: "The kings of old rewarded service and cherished kinsmen, enfeoffed younger brothers of the queen, and let them found houses of their own—so the royal line gained bulwarks against peril."

sentences.zh: 彰前受命北伐，清定朔土，厥功茂焉。

translations.literal: Zhang previously received orders for the northern campaign, cleared and settled the northern soil; his merit was luxuriant therein.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang, ordered north, pacified the frontier; his service was outstanding.

sentences.zh: 增邑五千，并前萬戶。

translations.literal: Increase his fief by five thousand households; together with the previous, ten thousand households."
translations.idiomatic: His appanage is increased by five thousand households, for a total of ten thousand.

sentences.zh: 』黃初二年，進爵為公。

translations.literal: In the second year of Huangchu, his noble rank was advanced to duke.
translations.idiomatic: In 221 his rank was raised to duke.

sentences.zh: 三年，立為任城王。

translations.literal: In the third year, he was established as King of Rencheng.
translations.idiomatic: In 222 he was invested as King of Rencheng.

sentences.zh: 四年，朝京都，疾薨於邸，謚曰威。

translations.literal: In the fourth year, he attended the capital; ill, he died in his lodging; posthumous name Wei.
translations.idiomatic: In 223 he came to court for an audience, fell ill in his residence, and died; he was posthumously titled Wei, "the Formidable."

sentences.zh: 〈魏氏春秋曰：初，彰問璽綬，將有異志，故來朝不即得見。

translations.literal: 〈The Wei shi chunqiu states: At first, when Zhang inquired about the seal-cord, he was about to have a different intent; therefore when he came to court he was not immediately permitted audience.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Wei Annals of Spring and Autumn claim that Zhang asked after the imperial seal with designs of his own, and for that reason was kept waiting when he presented himself at court.〉

sentences.zh: 彰忿怒暴薨。〉

translations.literal: Zhang, resentful and angry, suddenly died.〉
translations.idiomatic: He died suddenly, still in a rage.〉

sentences.zh: 至葬，賜鑾輅、龍旂，虎賁百人，如漢東平王故事。

translations.literal: At the time of burial, he was granted the imperial bell-carriage, dragon banners, and a hundred tiger-guardsmen, according to the precedent of the Han Prince of Dongping.
translations.idiomatic: For his funeral he received the bell-adorned hearse, dragon banners, and a hundred household guards, by the same honor once paid the Han Prince of Dongping.

sentences.zh: 子楷嗣，徙封中牟。

translations.literal: His son Kai succeeded and was transferred in enfeoffment to Zhongmou.
translations.idiomatic: His son Cao Kai inherited the title and was moved to the Zhongmou fief.

sentences.zh: 五年，改封任城縣。

translations.literal: In the fifth year, his enfeoffment was changed to Rencheng county.
translations.idiomatic: In 224 the fief was redesignated as Rencheng County.

sentences.zh: 太和六年，復改封任城國，食五縣二千五百戶。

translations.literal: In the sixth year of Taihe, it was again changed to the state of Rencheng, with food-revenue of five counties and two thousand five hundred households.
translations.idiomatic: In 232 he was re-established as Prince of the state of Rencheng, with income from five counties totaling twenty-five hundred households.

sentences.zh: 青龍三年，楷坐私遣官屬詣中尚方作禁物，削縣二千戶。

translations.literal: In the third year of Qinglong, Kai, sitting for privately dispatching official subordinates to the palace Ateliers to make forbidden objects, had two thousand households of a county stripped.
translations.idiomatic: In 235 Cao Kai lost two thousand households of his fief for secretly sending his staff to the imperial workshops to commission forbidden goods.

sentences.zh: 正始七年，徙封濟南，三千戶。

translations.literal: In the seventh year of Zhengshi, he was transferred in enfeoffment to Jinan, three thousand households.
translations.idiomatic: In 246 he was transferred to Jinan with a fief of three thousand households.

sentences.zh: 正元、景元初，連增邑，凡四千四百戶。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Zhengyuan and Jingyuan, his fief was continuously increased; in all four thousand four hundred households.
translations.idiomatic: Under Cao Mao and Cao Huan his appanage was enlarged in steps until it stood at forty-four hundred households.

sentences.zh: 〈楷，泰始初為崇化少府，見百官名。〉

translations.literal: 〈Kai, at the beginning of Taishi, was Junior Chamberlain for Exalting Transformation; see the roster of officials.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈Cao Kai served as Junior Chamberlain for Exalting Transformation at the start of the Jin dynasty; see the official lists.〉

sentences.zh: 陳思王曹植

translations.literal: The Prince of Chensi, Cao Zhi.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhi, Prince of Chensi.

sentences.zh: 陳思王植字子建。

translations.literal: The Prince of Chensi, Zhi, had the courtesy name Zijian.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhi, posthumously honored as Prince Si of Chen, bore the courtesy name Zijian.

sentences.zh: 年十歲餘，誦讀《詩》、《論》及辭賦數十萬言，善屬文。

translations.literal: At age a bit over ten years, he recited from memory the Shijing, Lunyu, and several hundred thousand words of rhapsodies and fu; he was skilled at composing texts.
translations.idiomatic: Before he was eleven he had memorized the Odes, the Analects, and hundreds of thousands of characters of verse and rhapsody, and he wrote with uncommon ease.

sentences.zh: 太祖嘗視其文，謂植曰：『汝倩人邪？

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor once examined his writing and said to Zhi, "Did you employ another person?"
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao once looked over his compositions and asked, "Did someone else write this for you?"

sentences.zh: 』植跪曰：『言出為論，下筆成章，顧當面試，柰何倩人？

translations.literal: Zhi knelt and said, "When words issue they become disquisitions; when the brush descends it completes chapters; I ask to be examined face to face—how could I employ another person?"
translations.idiomatic: Zhi knelt and answered: "I speak in finished argument and write in finished periods; put me to the test in your presence—why would I need a ghostwriter?"

sentences.zh: 』時鄴銅爵臺新成，太祖悉將諸子登臺，使各為賦。

translations.literal: At that time Ye's Bronze Bird Terrace was newly completed; the Grand Progenitor led all his sons to ascend the terrace and had each compose a fu.
translations.idiomatic: Just then the new Bronze Bird Terrace at Ye was finished; Cao Cao took every son up the stairs and set each to compose a rhapsody on the spot.

sentences.zh: 植援筆立成，可觀，太祖甚異之。

translations.literal: Zhi grasped the brush and completed it standing; it was worth viewing; the Grand Progenitor greatly marveled at him.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi seized a brush and finished at once; the piece was striking, and Cao Cao was deeply impressed.

sentences.zh: 〈陰澹《魏紀》載植賦曰『從明后而嬉游兮，登層台以娛情。

translations.literal: 〈Yin Dan's Wei ji records Zhi's fu, saying, "Following the enlightened later ruler in roaming play, ascending layered terraces to delight the feelings."
translations.idiomatic: 〈Yin Dan's Wei Records preserves Zhi's rhapsody: "I follow my enlightened lord in sport and climb tiered towers to lift the heart."

sentences.zh: 見太府之廣開兮，觀聖德之所營。

translations.literal: Beholding the Grand Storehouse's broad opening, observing where sagely virtue has built."
translations.idiomatic: I gaze on the great halls thrown wide and on the works that sacred virtue has raised."

sentences.zh: 建高門之嵯峨兮，浮雙闕乎太清。

translations.literal: Raising the high gate's towering height, floating twin gate-towers in the Grand Clarity."
translations.idiomatic: Lofty gates rear skyward; paired watchtowers ride the azure void."

sentences.zh: 立中天之華觀兮，連飛閣乎西城。

translations.literal: Establishing a splendid lookout amid heaven's center, linking soaring galleries toward the western wall."
translations.idiomatic: A splendid belvedere crowns mid-heaven; flying galleries span toward the city's west."

sentences.zh: 臨漳水之長流兮，望園果之滋榮。

translations.literal: Overlooking the Zhang River's long flow, gazing on the garden fruits' lush flourishing."
translations.idiomatic: Below lies the long roll of the Zhang; before me the orchards swell with fruit."

sentences.zh: 仰春風之和穆兮，聽百鳥之悲鳴。

translations.literal: Looking up to the spring wind's harmony and mildness, listening to the hundred birds' mournful cries."
translations.idiomatic: The spring wind breathes soft above; a hundred birds weave their plaintive song."

sentences.zh: 天雲垣其既立兮，家願得而獲逞。

translations.literal: Heaven's clouds as a rampart have already been established; the family's wishes obtain and achieve display."
translations.idiomatic: Heaven's clouds stand like a wall; the house of Cao may now fulfill its long desire."

sentences.zh: 揚仁化於宇內兮，盡肅恭於上京。

translations.literal: Raising humane transformation within the realm, exhausting reverent respect in the upper capital."
translations.idiomatic: Human kindness spreads through the realm; all the capital bends in reverent awe."

sentences.zh: 惟桓文之為盛兮，豈足方乎聖明！

translations.literal: Only Huan and Wen as being flourishing—how could they suffice to match sagely brilliance!"
translations.idiomatic: Huan and Wen were hailed as great—yet what are they beside our sage lord's light!"

sentences.zh: 休矣美矣！

translations.literal: How excellent! How beautiful!
translations.idiomatic: Grace upon grace, beauty upon beauty!

sentences.zh: 惠澤遠揚。

translations.literal: Kind favor is spread far.
translations.idiomatic: His kindly favor reaches to the horizon.

sentences.zh: 翼佐我皇家兮，寧彼四方。

translations.literal: Wing-assisting our imperial house, bringing peace to those four directions."
translations.idiomatic: He props our royal house on pinions and stills the four quarters of the world."

sentences.zh: 同天地之規量兮，齊日月之暉光。

translations.literal: Same as heaven and earth's norm and measure, equal to sun and moon's radiant light."
translations.idiomatic: His measure matches heaven and earth; his splendor vies with sun and moon."

sentences.zh: 永貴尊而無極兮，等年壽於東王』云云。

translations.literal: Forever honored and venerated without limit, equal in years and longevity to the Eastern King," and so on.
translations.idiomatic: May he be honored without end and share the years of the King of the East," and more in that vein.

sentences.zh: 太祖深異之。〉

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor deeply marveled at him.〉
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao was struck with wonder.〉

sentences.zh: 性簡易，不治威儀。

translations.literal: By nature he was simple and easygoing; he did not cultivate awesome deportment.
translations.idiomatic: He was plain and unaffected by temperament and never put on lordly airs.

sentences.zh: 輿馬服飾，不尚華麗。

translations.literal: Carriages, horses, clothing, and adornments—he did not esteem splendor and beauty.
translations.idiomatic: His carriages, mounts, and dress favored modesty over display.

sentences.zh: 每進見難問，應聲而對，特見寵愛。

translations.literal: Whenever he advanced to audience and was questioned with difficulties, he answered following the sound of the voice; he was especially seen with favor and love.
translations.idiomatic: At each audience Cao Cao pressed him with hard questions, and he answered on the instant—hence he stood highest in his father's favor.

sentences.zh: 建安十六年，封平原侯。

translations.literal: In the sixteenth year of Jian'an, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Pingyuan.
translations.idiomatic: In 211 he became Marquis of Pingyuan.

sentences.zh: 十九年，徙封臨菑侯。

translations.literal: In the nineteenth year, his enfeoffment was transferred to Marquis of Linzi.
translations.idiomatic: In 214 his title was moved to Marquis of Linzi.

sentences.zh: 太祖征孫權，使植留守鄴，戒之曰：『吾昔為頓邱令，年二十三。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor campaigned against Sun Quan and ordered Zhi to remain guarding Ye, admonishing him, saying, "In the past I was magistrate of Dunqiu, age twenty-three.
translations.idiomatic: When Cao Cao marched against Sun Quan, he left Zhi to hold Ye and told him: "At twenty-three I was magistrate of Dunqiu.

sentences.zh: 思此時所行，無悔於今。

translations.literal: Reflecting on what I did at that time, I have no regret unto today.
translations.idiomatic: Looking back on how I carried myself then, I have nothing I would undo."

sentences.zh: 今汝年亦二十三矣，可不勉與！

translations.literal: Now your years are likewise twenty-three—can you not exert yourself!"
translations.idiomatic: You are the same age now—see that you do not fall short!"

sentences.zh: 』植既以才見異，而丁儀、丁廙、楊脩等為之羽翼。

translations.literal: Zhi had already been set apart for his talent, while Ding Yi, Ding Yi (Yi), Yang Xiu, and others formed his wings.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi’s gifts had already marked him out, and Ding Yi, Ding Yì, Yang Xiu, and others gathered round him as his partisans.

sentences.zh: 太祖狐疑，幾為太子者數矣。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor wavered; several times he came near making him heir.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao hesitated so often that Zhi nearly became heir more than once.

sentences.zh: 而植任性而行，不自彫勵，飲酒不節。

translations.literal: But Zhi followed his impulses and did not discipline himself; he drank without restraint.
translations.idiomatic: Yet Zhi followed his whims, refused to school himself, and drank without limit.

sentences.zh: 文帝御之以術，矯情自飾，宮人左右，併為之說，故遂定為嗣。

translations.literal: Emperor Wen managed affairs with calculation, disguised his feelings and polished his conduct, and those about the palace all spoke on his behalf; therefore he was at last fixed as successor.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Pi played the game with cold skill—masked his heart, trimmed his conduct, and won every voice in the harem to his side—until the succession was his.

sentences.zh: 二十二年，增置邑五千，並前萬戶。

translations.literal: In the twenty-second year, his fief was increased by five thousand households, together with the previous ten thousand.
translations.idiomatic: In 217 his income was raised by five thousand households, for the same ten thousand in all as before.

sentences.zh: 植嘗乘車行馳道中，開司馬門出。

translations.literal: Zhi once rode in a carriage along the imperial speedway and opened the Sima Gate to leave.
translations.idiomatic: Once Zhi drove his carriage down the forbidden carriage track and had the Sima Gate opened for his exit.

sentences.zh: 太祖大怒，公車令坐死。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor was greatly enraged; the superintendent of the Grand Carriage was sentenced to death for sitting (by negligence).
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao’s fury fell on the official who held the Sima Gate; the man was condemned to death.

sentences.zh: 由是重諸侯科禁，而植寵日衰。

translations.literal: From this the regulations restricting the feudal lords were strengthened, and Zhi’s favor daily waned.
translations.idiomatic: The rules binding the princes were tightened after that, and Zhi’s star sank day by day.

sentences.zh: 《魏武故事》載令曰：『始者謂子建，兒中最可定大事。

translations.literal: The Wei Wu gushi records an edict stating, “At first I said of Zijian that among my sons he was the one who could settle great affairs.”
translations.idiomatic: The Record of Wei Wu’s Administrative Acts quotes an edict: “I once thought Zijian the son who could shoulder the weightiest charge.”

sentences.zh: 』又令曰：『自臨菑侯植私出，開司馬門至金門，令吾異目視此兒矣。

translations.literal: Another edict states, “Since Marquis of Linzi Zhi went out without leave, opened the Sima Gate as far as the Golden Gate, it makes me look on this boy with different eyes.”
translations.idiomatic: Another reads: “When the Marquis of Linzi slipped out on his own and forced the Sima Gate clear to the Golden Gate, I began to see that son in another light.”

sentences.zh: 』又令曰：『諸侯長史及帳下吏，知吾出輒將諸侯行意否？

translations.literal: Another edict states, “Do the chief clerks of the princes and the officers under their tents know whether, whenever I go out, they always carry out the princes’ intentions?”
translations.idiomatic: A third asks: “Do those stewards and household officers know whether, each time I leave the palace, they still do the bidding of their lords?”

sentences.zh: 從子建私開司馬門來，吾都不覆信諸侯也。

translations.literal: “After Zijian’s private opening of the Sima Gate, I altogether no longer trust the princes.”
translations.idiomatic: “Since Zijian broke the Sima Gate on his own, I no longer place faith in any of the enfeoffed princes.”

sentences.zh: 恐吾適出，便復私出，故攝將行。

translations.literal: “I fear that just when I go out they will again go out privately; therefore I take them along when I go.”
translations.idiomatic: “I dread that the moment I step out they will steal out again—so I march them with me when I ride.”

sentences.zh: 不可恆使吾

translations.literal: “One cannot constantly make me
translations.idiomatic: “You cannot forever force me

translations.literal: (you)
translations.idiomatic: (you)

sentences.zh: 〔以〕誰為心腹也！

translations.literal: to treat whom as trusted confidants!”
translations.idiomatic: to name anyone my true confidant!”

sentences.zh: 』太祖既慮終始之變，以楊脩頗有才策，而又袁氏之甥也，於是以罪誅脩。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor, having already worried over changes from beginning to end, and because Yang Xiu was quite talented in stratagem and moreover was a nephew by marriage of the Yuan clan, therefore on a charge executed Xiu.
translations.idiomatic: Uneasy about what the end might bring, and knowing Yang Xiu for a clever schemer who was also tied by marriage to the Yuans, Cao Cao found a pretext and put him to death.

sentences.zh: 植益內不自安。

translations.literal: Zhi inwardly became ever more uneasy.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi grew more anxious by the day.

sentences.zh: 《典略》曰：楊脩字德祖，太尉彪子也。

translations.literal: The Dianlüe states: Yang Xiu, courtesy name Dezǔ, was a son of Grand Commandant Yang Biao.
translations.idiomatic: The Brief Account of Current Affairs says Yang Xiu (Dezǔ) was the son of Grand Commandant Yang Biao.

sentences.zh: 謙恭才博。

translations.literal: He was modest and respectful, and his talents were broad.
translations.idiomatic: He combined humility with wide learning.

sentences.zh: 建安中，舉孝廉，除郎中，丞相請署倉曹屬主簿。

translations.literal: In the Jian’an period he was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt, appointed Gentleman of the Palace, and the Chancellor requested him to serve as Registrar under the Granary Bureau.
translations.idiomatic: During Jian’an he entered office as Filial and Incorrupt, rose to Gentleman of the Palace, and was assigned registrar under the Chancellor’s Granary Bureau.

sentences.zh: 是時，軍國多事，脩總知外內，事皆稱意。

translations.literal: At that time military and state affairs were many; Xiu oversaw both inner and outer matters, and everything met with approval.
translations.idiomatic: With army and court both in turmoil, Xiu ran civil and military paperwork to Cao Cao’s satisfaction.

sentences.zh: 自魏太子已下，並爭與交好。

translations.literal: From the Wei heir downward, all vied to befriend him.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone from the heir of Wei downward scrambled to win his friendship.

sentences.zh: 又是時臨菑侯植以才捷愛幸，來意投脩，數與脩書，書曰：

translations.literal: Moreover at that time Marquis of Linzi Zhi, because of his quick talent, was loved and favored; his mind inclined toward Xiu, and several times he wrote to Xiu; the letter said,
translations.idiomatic: The Marquis of Linzi, favored for his ready wit, warmed to Xiu and wrote him often; one letter began:

sentences.zh: 數日不見，思子為勞；

translations.literal: Several days without seeing you—I think of you and grow weary;
translations.idiomatic: A few days apart, and I am worn thin with longing;

sentences.zh: 想同之也。

translations.literal: I suppose you feel the same.
translations.idiomatic: I imagine you feel the same.

sentences.zh: 僕少好詞賦，迄至于今二十有五年矣。

translations.literal: I have loved rhapsodies since youth; down to today it has been twenty-five years.
translations.idiomatic: I have loved verse and rhapsody since I was a boy—twenty-five years now.

sentences.zh: 然今世作者，可略而言也。

translations.literal: Yet the writers of this age may be spoken of in outline.
translations.idiomatic: The authors of our time can be summed up in a word or two.

sentences.zh: 昔仲宣獨步於漢南，孔璋鷹揚於河朔，偉長擅名於青土，公幹振藻於海隅，德璉發跡於大魏，足下高視於上京。

translations.literal: Formerly Zhongxuan walked alone south of the Han; Kongzhang soared like a hawk north of the He; Weichang made a name in Qing soil; Gongqian shook his brilliance at the sea’s edge; Delian rose in Great Wei; you, sir, held your gaze high in the upper capital.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Can strode unrivalled south of the Han; Chen Lin hunted like a hawk in Hebei; Xu Gan won his laurels in the eastern hills; Liu Zhen flashed his colors on the coast; Ying Yang made his start in Wei; and you, sir, looked down from the imperial city.

sentences.zh: 當此之時，人人自謂握靈蛇之珠，家家自謂抱荊山之玉也。

translations.literal: At that time each man claimed to grasp the pearl of the spirit serpent; each house claimed to embrace the jade of Jingshan.
translations.idiomatic: Then every man swore he held the pearl of the magic snake; every house boasted the jade of Mount Jing.

sentences.zh: 吾王於是設天網以該之，頓八紘以掩之，今盡集茲國矣。

translations.literal: Thereupon our king spread heaven’s net to encompass them, shook the eight cords to cover them; now all are gathered in this state.
translations.idiomatic: Our prince cast the net of heaven, drew in the eight directions, and now they are all assembled here in Wei.

sentences.zh: 然此數子，猶不能飛翰絕跡，一舉千里也。

translations.literal: Yet these several men still could not cut their brush-strokes and leave no trace, rising in one leap a thousand li.
translations.idiomatic: Even so, not one of them has quite cleared the traces of his brush or soared a thousand li at a single stroke.

sentences.zh: 以孔璋之才，不閑辭賦，而多自謂與司馬長卿同風，譬畫虎不成還為狗者也。

translations.literal: With Kongzhang’s talent, he was not versed in rhapsody, yet often claimed for himself the same air as Sima Xiangru—like one who tries to paint a tiger and ends with a dog.
translations.idiomatic: Chen Lin has no gift for fu, yet he keeps comparing himself to Sima Xiangru—like the painter who set out to draw a tiger and produced a cur instead.

sentences.zh: 前為書啁之，反作論盛道僕贊其文。

translations.literal: Earlier I wrote to tease him; he turned it into a treatise loudly praising me for admiring his writing.
translations.idiomatic: I mocked him in a letter; he answered with a long essay insisting I had praised his prose.

sentences.zh: 夫鍾期不失聽，于今稱之。

translations.literal: When Zhong Ziqi never misheard a note, posterity still praises him.
translations.idiomatic: Bo Ya’s ear for music is still remembered.

sentences.zh: 吾亦不敢妄歎者，畏後之嗤余也。

translations.literal: I also dare not praise at random, fearing those who come after will laugh at me.
translations.idiomatic: I dare not hand out empty praise, lest later ages snicker at me.

sentences.zh: 世人著述，不能無病。

translations.literal: The writings of men in the world cannot be without flaws.
translations.idiomatic: No book under heaven is free of fault.

sentences.zh: 僕常好人譏彈其文；

translations.literal: I have always liked having others pick apart my texts;
translations.idiomatic: I have always welcomed criticism of my drafts;

sentences.zh: 有不善者，應時改定。

translations.literal: where something is not good, I correct it on the spot.
translations.idiomatic: and when a line fails, I mend it at once.

sentences.zh: 昔丁敬禮嘗作小文，使僕潤飾之，僕自以才不能過若人，辭不為也。

translations.literal: Formerly Ding Jingli once composed a short piece and had me polish it; I myself thought my talent could not surpass that man and declined to do it.
translations.idiomatic: Once Ding Jingli asked me to touch up a short piece; I thought I could not outwrite the man and refused.

sentences.zh: 敬禮云：「卿何所疑難乎！

translations.literal: Jingli said, “What doubt troubles you!
translations.idiomatic: Jingli said: “Why hesitate?

sentences.zh: 文之佳麗，吾自得之。

translations.literal: The beauty of the text—I obtain it myself.
translations.idiomatic: The fine phrases are mine in any case.

sentences.zh: 後世誰相知定吾文者邪？

translations.literal: Who in later ages will know me well enough to fix my writing?”
translations.idiomatic: Who after we are gone will be the judge who “fixes” my lines?”

sentences.zh: 」吾常嘆此達言，以為美談。

translations.literal: I have always sighed at this enlightened saying and taken it for a fine tale.
translations.idiomatic: I have treasured that wise remark as a model ever since.

sentences.zh: 昔尼父之文辭，與人通流；

translations.literal: Formerly the literary phrasing of the Master shared the common current with others;
translations.idiomatic: Confucius’s ordinary essays flowed with the speech of his day;

sentences.zh: 至於制《春秋》，游、夏之徒不能錯一字。

translations.literal: but when it came to composing the Chunqiu, even disciples like You and Xia could not alter a single character.
translations.idiomatic: but when he forged the Spring and Autumn Annals, not even Ziyou and Zixia could change one word.

sentences.zh: 過此而言不病者，吾未之見也。

translations.literal: Beyond this, to say one’s writing has no faults—I have not seen such a person.
translations.idiomatic: Claim flawless prose beyond that—I have never met the man.

sentences.zh: 蓋有南威之容，乃可以論於淑媛；

translations.literal: Only if one has the looks of Nanwei may one discuss graceful ladies;
translations.idiomatic: You must have Nanwei’s face before you lecture on beauty;

sentences.zh: 有龍淵之利，乃可以議於割斷。

translations.literal: only if one has the sharpness of Longyuan may one debate cutting clean.
translations.idiomatic: you must wield the Longyuan blade before you discourse on the cleaving stroke.

sentences.zh: 劉季緒才不逮於作者，而好詆呵文章，掎摭利病。

translations.literal: Liu Jixu’s talent does not reach that of a real author, yet he loves to slander writing and seize on flaws.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xiu is no writer, yet he delights in tearing apart other men’s lines and hunting for blemishes.

sentences.zh: 昔田巴毀五帝，罪三王，呰五伯於稷下，一旦而服千人，魯連一說，使終身杜口。

translations.literal: Formerly Tian Ba reviled the Five Emperors, blamed the Three Kings, and sneered at the Five Hegemons below Jixia; in a single day he overawed a thousand men—yet one speech from Lu Lian left him dumb for life.
translations.idiomatic: Tian Ba once vilified the Five Thearchs, the Three Kings, and the Five Lords at Jixia and silenced a thousand hearers in a day—until Lu Zhonglian spoke once and he never opened his mouth again.

sentences.zh: 劉生之辯未若田氏，今之仲連求之不難，可無嘆息乎！

translations.literal: Liu Sheng’s eloquence does not match Tian’s; to find today’s Zhonglian for him would not be hard—can one help sighing!
translations.idiomatic: Liu’s rhetoric falls short of Tian Ba’s; a modern Lu Lian would soon put him down—small wonder one groans at the sight.

sentences.zh: 人各有所好尚。

translations.literal: Each man has what he loves and esteems.
translations.idiomatic: Tastes differ with every man.

sentences.zh: 蘭茝蓀蕙之芳，眾人之所好，而海畔有逐臭之夫；

translations.literal: The fragrance of thoroughwort, iris, and sweet flag is what the crowd loves, yet by the sea there is a man who chases stench;
translations.idiomatic: The world loves orchid and iris, yet some coast-dweller craves the smell of rot;

sentences.zh: 《咸池》、《六英》之發，眾人所樂，而墨翟有非之之論：豈可同哉！

translations.literal: the tones of Xianchi and Liuying are what the multitude delights in, yet Mozi had arguments against them—how can things be the same!
translations.idiomatic: the world thrills to Xianchi and Liuying, yet Mozi condemned them—how can all hearts agree!

sentences.zh: 今往僕少小所著詞賦一通相與。

translations.literal: Now I send you in one bundle the rhapsodies I wrote in my youth.
translations.idiomatic: I enclose a packet of the verse I composed in my younger days.

sentences.zh: 夫街談巷說，必有可采，擊轅之歌，有應風雅，匹夫之思，未易輕棄也。

translations.literal: Street talk and lane gossip surely has something worth taking; songs struck on wagon-yokes may answer to the Feng and Ya; the thoughts of a common man are not to be lightly cast aside.
translations.idiomatic: Market gossip holds grains of truth; songs banged out on a cart-shaft can match the Odes; a plain fellow’s notion is not to be despised.

sentences.zh: 辭賦小道，固未足以揄揚大義，彰示來世也。

translations.literal: Rhapsody is a minor path; it is indeed not enough to exalt great principles or display them to later ages.
translations.idiomatic: Fu is a side road—it cannot proclaim the great Way or instruct posterity.

sentences.zh: 昔揚子雲，先朝執戟之臣耳，猶稱「壯夫不為」也；

translations.literal: Formerly Yang Ziyun was merely a halberd-bearer of the former court, yet still said, “A stalwart does not do such things”;
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiong was only a court guardsman, yet he said, “A full-grown man does not traffic in this”;

sentences.zh: 吾雖薄德，位為藩侯，猶庶幾戮力上國，流惠下民，建永世之業，流金石之功，豈徒以翰墨為勳績，辭頌為君子哉？

translations.literal: though my virtue is slight, my rank is that of a frontier prince; I still hope to strain my strength for the upper state, spread kindness on the people below, found an enterprise for all time, and leave merit carved in metal and stone—how could I take brush and ink alone as achievement, or hymns and odes as the mark of a gentleman?
translations.idiomatic: I am a minor prince, yet I mean to serve the throne, bless my people, build a lasting work, and win fame on bronze and stone—not to make a career of ink alone or call myself a gentleman because I chant pretty lines.

sentences.zh: 若吾志不果，吾道不行，亦將採史官之實錄，辯時俗之得失，定仁義之衷，成一家之言，雖未能藏之名山，將以傳之同好，此要之白首，豈可以今日論乎！

translations.literal: If my aims are not realized and my Way does not prevail, I will still gather the true records of the historians, distinguish gain and loss in the customs of the age, fix the mean between benevolence and righteousness, and complete the words of one school—though I may not hide them on a famous mountain, I will pass them to those who share my taste; this is the business of a white head—how can it be judged by this day alone!
translations.idiomatic: If I fail in that aim, I will still quarry the historians’ annals, weigh the age’s right and wrong, set the balance of humaneness and duty, and speak in my own voice—if not to hide the book on a sacred hill, then at least to share it with kindred spirits; that is work for a lifetime, not something to settle in a morning’s talk.

sentences.zh: 其言之不怍，恃惠子之知我也。

translations.literal: That my words are not shameless rests on Huizi’s knowing me.
translations.idiomatic: I speak without blushing because I trust you to understand me as Huizi understood Zhuangzi.

sentences.zh: 明早相迎，書不盡懷。

translations.literal: I will welcome you tomorrow morning; the letter cannot exhaust what is in my heart.
translations.idiomatic: I shall expect you at dawn; ink cannot hold all I feel.

sentences.zh: 脩答曰：

translations.literal: Xiu replied,
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiu answered:

sentences.zh: 不侍數日，若彌年載，豈獨愛顧之隆，使係仰之情深邪！

translations.literal: Without waiting several days, it is as if a year had passed—is it only the height of your loving regard that makes my yearning so deep!
translations.idiomatic: A few days’ silence feels like a year—is it only your kindness that binds my heart so fast!

sentences.zh: 損辱來命，蔚矣其文。

translations.literal: I have received your honored command; its text is luxuriant.
translations.idiomatic: Your letter humbles me; its lines glow with color.

sentences.zh: 誦讀反覆，雖《風》、《雅》、《頌》，不復過也。

translations.literal: Reading it back and forth, even the Feng, Ya, and Song could not surpass it.
translations.idiomatic: Read and reread, it outshines even the Airs, the Elegantiae, and the Hymns.

sentences.zh: 若仲宣之擅江表，陳氏之跨冀域，徐、劉之顯青、豫，應生之發魏國，斯皆然矣。

translations.literal: As for Zhongxuan’s mastery south of the Yangzi, the Chen clan’s stride across Ji, Xu and Liu’s fame in Qing and Yu, and Master Ying’s rise in Wei—all this is so.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Can’s mastery south of the Yangzi, the Chen name in Ji, Xu Gan and Liu Zhen’s reputations in Qing and Yu, Ying Yang’s rise in Wei—you have the right of it all.

sentences.zh: 至如脩者，聽采風聲，仰德不暇，目周章於省覽，何惶駭於高視哉？

translations.literal: As for one like Xiu, who listens to rumor and has no leisure to look up to virtue, my eyes wander in reviewing—how should I be awestruck at lofty vision?
translations.idiomatic: For my own part I catch only rumor and scarce lift my eyes to true greatness—how should I gape like one dazzled by a summit?

sentences.zh: 伏惟君侯，少長貴盛，體旦、發之質，有聖善之教。

translations.literal: I humbly reflect that you, my lord, from youth have been noble and flourishing, embody the substance of Dan and Fa, and have received instruction in sagely goodness.
translations.idiomatic: You, sir, were born to rank and bred on the models of the Duke of Zhou and Dan, the Duke of Shao.

sentences.zh: 遠近觀者，徒謂能宣昭懿德，光贊大業而已，不謂復能兼覽傳記，留思文章。

translations.literal: Those who watch from afar merely say you can proclaim bright virtue and illumine the great enterprise; they do not say you can also read transmitted records and fix your mind on literary craft.
translations.idiomatic: Onlookers thought you would only broadcast virtue and magnify the dynasty; they did not expect you to devour histories and brood over style.

sentences.zh: 今乃含王超陳，度越數子；

translations.literal: Now you embrace the kings and surpass Chen, leaping past these several men;
translations.idiomatic: Now you outrun the kings of verse and leave Chen Lin behind;

sentences.zh: 觀者駭視而拭目，聽者傾首而聳耳；

translations.literal: watchers wipe their eyes in wonder, listeners crane their necks and prick their ears;
translations.idiomatic: spectators rub their eyes, hearers strain their ears;

sentences.zh: 非夫體通性達，受之自然，其誰能至於此乎？

translations.literal: if one has not embodied the Way and comprehended nature, receiving it from what is natural, who could reach this?
translations.idiomatic: who could reach such heights without native penetration of the Way?

sentences.zh: 又嘗親見執事握牘持筆，有所造作，若成誦在心，借書於手，曾不斯須少留思慮。

translations.literal: Moreover I have personally seen you, brush in hand over the writing-slip, composing—if it were recitation fixed in the heart and borrowing the book in the hand, you never paused a moment for thought.
translations.idiomatic: I have watched you seize brush and tablet and write as though the text were already memorized—never a second’s hesitation.

sentences.zh: 仲尼日月，無得逾焉。

translations.literal: Zhongni is sun and moon; none may overstep him.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius is sun and moon; none may eclipse him.

sentences.zh: 脩之仰望，殆如此矣。

translations.literal: Xiu’s gazing upward is almost like this.
translations.idiomatic: So I look up to you.

sentences.zh: 是以對鶡而辭，作《暑賦》彌日而不獻，見西施之容，歸憎其貌者也。

translations.literal: Therefore I declined before the heron and, composing the “Summer Heat” rhapsody, did not present it for a whole day—like one who, having seen Xishi’s face, returns loathing his own looks.
translations.idiomatic: So I hid my face before the heron and, though I drafted a fu on the summer heat, would not show it for a day—like a man who hates his own looks after glimpsing Xishi.

sentences.zh: 伏想執事不知其然，猥受顧賜，教使刊定。

translations.literal: I humbly suppose you, my lord, did not realize this; wrongly receiving your favor, you ordered me to revise and fix it.
translations.idiomatic: I fear you did not know my shame; you honored me with a command to polish your lines.

sentences.zh: 《春秋》之成，莫能損益。

translations.literal: When the Chunqiu was complete, none could add or subtract.
translations.idiomatic: Once the Spring and Autumn Annals stood complete, no hand could alter a word.

sentences.zh: 《呂氏》、《淮南》，字直千金；

translations.literal: The Lüshi chunqiu and Huainanzi—each character worth a thousand in gold;
translations.idiomatic: The Lü’s Spring and Autumn and the Huainan—every word worth its weight in gold;

sentences.zh: 然而弟子鉗口，市人拱手者，聖賢卓犖，固所以殊絕凡庸也。

translations.literal: yet the disciples sealed their lips and the market crowd folded their hands—because sages and worthies stand supreme, this is indeed how they differ from the common run.
translations.idiomatic: yet their disciples dared not breathe a correction—so it is when a sage towers above the crowd.

sentences.zh: 今之賦頌，古詩之流，不更孔公，風雅無別耳。

translations.literal: Today’s fu and eulogies are of the same stream as ancient poetry; unless they pass through Master Kong, there is no distinction from the Feng and Ya.
translations.idiomatic: Modern fu descend from the old songs; without Confucius’s touch they are not true Airs and Odes.

sentences.zh: 脩家子雲，老不曉事，彊著一書，悔其少作。

translations.literal: Xiu’s householder Ziyun, old and not understanding affairs, forced himself to write one book and regretted his youthful work.
translations.idiomatic: Your servant’s townsman Yang Xiong, foolish in old age, forced out one book and repented his early writings.

sentences.zh: 若此，仲山、周旦之徒，則皆有愆乎！

translations.literal: If it were so, would even Zhongshan and Zhou Dan all have faults!
translations.idiomatic: If that were the rule, even the Duke of Zhou would stand condemned!

sentences.zh: 君侯忘聖賢之顯跡，述鄙宗之過言，竊以為未之思也。

translations.literal: You, my lord, forget the plain traces of sages and worthies and repeat the shallow words of my humble clan—I privately think you have not reflected on this.
translations.idiomatic: You cite my humble lineage’s gossip and forget how the sages behaved—I think you have not weighed that.

sentences.zh: 若乃不忘經國之大美，流千載之英聲，銘功景鍾，書名竹帛，此自雅量素所蓄也，豈與文章相妨害哉？

translations.literal: As for not forgetting the great beauty of ordering the state, spreading a splendid name for a thousand ages, inscribing merit on the Jing bell, and writing one’s name on bamboo and silk—these are what your magnanimous nature has long stored up; how could they obstruct literary work?
translations.idiomatic: To mind the great work of state, ring your fame on the Jing bell, and carve your name in history—that is the purpose you have always cherished; it does not clash with letters.

sentences.zh: 輒受所惠，竊備矇瞍誦歌而已。

translations.literal: I have received what you bestowed and humbly prepare only to chant like the blind.
translations.idiomatic: I accept your gift and can only mumble praise like a blind man singing.

sentences.zh: 敢忘惠施，以忝莊氏！

translations.literal: How dare I forget Huizi and disgrace Zhuangzi!
translations.idiomatic: I would not slight Huizi and shame Zhuang Zhou.

sentences.zh: 季緒瑣瑣，何足以云。

translations.literal: Jixu is petty—how can he be worth mentioning!
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xiu is too small a man to name.

sentences.zh: 二十四年，曹仁為關羽所圍。

translations.literal: In the twenty-fourth year, Cao Ren was besieged by Guan Yu.
translations.idiomatic: In 219 Cao Ren was trapped by Guan Yu.

sentences.zh: 太祖以植為南中郎將，行征虜將軍，欲遣救仁，呼有所敕戒。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor appointed Zhi General of the Household for the South and acting General Who Subdues Captives, intending to dispatch him to rescue Ren, and summoned him to give instructions and warnings.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao named Zhi acting General Who Subdues Captives and General of the Household for the South, meant to send him to relieve Ren, and called him in for his orders.

sentences.zh: 植醉不能受命，於是悔而罷之。

translations.literal: Zhi was drunk and could not receive the command; thereupon he regretted it and dismissed the matter.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi was too drunk to take the commission; Cao Cao repented of the plan and dropped it.

sentences.zh: 〈《魏氏春秋》曰：植將行，太子飲焉，偪而醉之。

translations.literal: 〈The Wei shi chunqiu states: When Zhi was about to depart, the Heir Apparent gave him drink and forced him until he was drunk.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Wei Annals of Spring and Autumn say the heir poured wine for Zhi and made him drunk before he rode out.〉

sentences.zh: 王召植，植不能受王命，故王怒也。〉

translations.literal: The king summoned Zhi; Zhi could not receive the king’s command; therefore the king was angry.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈When the king called for Zhi, he could not answer the summons—hence the king’s wrath.〉

sentences.zh: 文帝即王位，誅丁儀、丁廙并其男口。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wen assumed the kingly throne, he executed Ding Yi and Ding Yi (Yi) together with their male dependents.
translations.idiomatic: As soon as Cao Pi became King of Wei, he put Ding Yi, Ding Yì, and every male in their houses to death.

sentences.zh: 〈《魏略》曰：◎丁儀字正禮，沛郡人也。

translations.literal: 〈The Weilüe states: ◎ Ding Yi, courtesy name Zhengli, was a man of Pei commandery.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Weilüe: Ding Yi (Zhengli) came from Pei.〉

sentences.zh: 父沖，宿與太祖親善，時隨乘輿。

translations.literal: His father Chong had long been on close terms with the Grand Progenitor and at times rode in the imperial carriage.
translations.idiomatic: His father Ding Chong had long been intimate with Cao Cao and sometimes rode in the imperial equipage.

sentences.zh: 見國家未定，乃與太祖書曰：『足下平生常喟然有匡佐之志，今其時矣。

translations.literal: Seeing the state not yet settled, he wrote to the Grand Progenitor, saying, “All your life you have often sighed with the ambition to aid and support; now is the time.”
translations.idiomatic: Seeing the realm still unsettled, he wrote: “You have always burned to set the world to rights; the moment is now.”

sentences.zh: 』是時張楊適還河內，太祖得其書，乃引軍迎天子東詣許，以沖為司隸校尉。

translations.literal: At that time Zhang Yang had just returned to Henei; the Grand Progenitor obtained his letter and thereupon led the army to welcome the Son of Heaven east to Xu, appointing Chong Colonel Director of Retainers.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Yang had just withdrawn to Henei; Cao Cao read the letter, marched to escort the emperor east to Xu, and made Ding Chong Colonel Director of Retainers.

sentences.zh: 後數來過諸將飲，酒美不能止，醉爛腸死。

translations.literal: Afterward he repeatedly came to drink with the various generals; the wine was fine and he could not stop; drunk, his intestines rotted and he died.
translations.idiomatic: He kept joining the commanders for feasts, could not refuse the cup, and drank himself to death—his belly literally torn apart by wine.

sentences.zh: 太祖以沖前見開導，常德之。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor because Chong had earlier opened the way with counsel, always thought kindly of him.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao remembered how Ding Chong had first urged him to take the emperor in hand, and held him in lasting regard.

sentences.zh: 聞儀為令士，雖未見，欲以愛女妻之，以問五官將。

translations.literal: Hearing that Yi was an outstanding gentleman, though he had not yet seen him, he wished to marry his beloved daughter to him, and asked the General of the Five Offices.
translations.idiomatic: Learning that Ding Yi was a man of parts, though they had never met, Cao Cao meant to give him a princess for wife and took the matter to the heir.

sentences.zh: 五官將曰：『女人觀貌，而正禮目不便，誠恐愛女未必悅也。

translations.literal: The General of the Five Offices said, "Women look at faces, and Zhengli’s eyes are not comely; I truly fear your beloved daughter may not be pleased."
translations.idiomatic: Cao Pi answered: "Women judge by looks; Ding Yi’s eyes are weak—I doubt our sister would be happy with the match."

sentences.zh: 以為不如與伏波子楙。

translations.literal: He thought it better to give her to Mao, son of the general who bore the title Who Crosses the Waves."
translations.idiomatic: He urged you to betroth her instead to Mao, son of the old Fubo general."

sentences.zh: 』太祖從之。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor followed this.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao took his advice.

sentences.zh: 尋闢儀為掾，到與論議，嘉其才朗，曰：『丁掾，好士也，即使其兩目盲，尚當與女，何況但眇？

translations.literal: Soon he summoned Yi as aide; when he arrived and they debated, he praised his bright talent, saying, "Aide Ding is a lover of fine men—even were both his eyes blind, I would still give him my daughter; how much more when he is only squinting?"
translations.idiomatic: Soon Ding Yi was called in as an adviser; one conversation won Cao Cao over. "Ding Yi loves talent," he cried. "I would marry my daughter to him if he were wholly blind—what is a squint?"

sentences.zh: 是吾兒誤我。

translations.literal: This is my son who misled me."
translations.idiomatic: My son misled me on this."

sentences.zh: 』時儀亦恨不得尚公主，而與臨菑侯親善，數稱其奇才。

translations.literal: At that time Yi also regretted not being able to marry a princess, but was on close terms with Marquis of Linzi and often praised his extraordinary talent.
translations.idiomatic: Ding Yi bitterly regretted missing the princess, but he clung to the Marquis of Linzi and never tired of praising Zhi’s genius.

sentences.zh: 太祖既有意欲立植，而儀又共贊之。

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor already had the intention of establishing Zhi, and Yi moreover together supported him.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao already leaned toward naming Zhi heir, and Ding Yi pushed the same way.

sentences.zh: 及太子立，欲治儀罪，轉儀為右刺姦掾，欲儀自裁而儀不能。

translations.literal: When the Heir Apparent was established, he wished to punish Yi; he transferred Yi to Right Clerk Who Investigates Treachery, wishing Yi would take his own life, but Yi could not.
translations.idiomatic: Once Cao Pi was heir, he moved to ruin Ding Yi, shunted him into the post of right “thorn-investigator,” and hoped shame would drive him to suicide—but Ding Yi could not do it.

sentences.zh: 乃對中領軍夏侯尚叩頭求哀，尚為涕泣而不能救。

translations.literal: Thereupon he knocked his head to the ground begging pity before Colonel of the Central Army Xiahou Shang; Shang wept for him but could not save him.
translations.idiomatic: He threw himself at Xiahou Shang’s feet and begged; Shang wept yet could not shield him.

sentences.zh: 後遂因職事收付獄，殺之。

translations.literal: Later then on official business he was seized and delivered to prison and killed.
translations.idiomatic: Soon a charge was fabricated, he was clapped in irons, and put to death.

sentences.zh: ◎廙字敬禮，儀之弟也。

translations.literal: ◎ Yì, courtesy name Jingli, was Yi’s younger brother.
translations.idiomatic: Ding Yì (courtesy Jingli) was Ding Yi’s younger brother.

sentences.zh: 《文士傳》曰：廙少有才姿，博學洽聞。

translations.literal: The Biographies of Literary Men states: Yì in youth had fine talent and bearing, broad learning and wide knowledge.
translations.idiomatic: The Record of Men of Letters says Ding Yì was gifted in youth, read everything, and heard everything.

sentences.zh: 初闢公府，建安中為黃門侍郎。

translations.literal: At first he was summoned to the Duke’s offices; in the Jian’an period he served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gates.
translations.idiomatic: He first entered Cao Cao’s bureau, then rose to Gentleman of the Yellow Gates under Jian’an.

sentences.zh: 廙嘗從容謂太祖曰：『臨菑侯天性仁孝，發於自然，而聰明智達，其殆庶幾。

translations.literal: Yì once calmly said to the Grand Progenitor, "Marquis of Linzi by nature is humane and filial, arising from what is natural, and in cleverness and wisdom he is penetrating—he is almost there."
translations.idiomatic: Once Ding Yì told Cao Cao plainly: "The Marquis of Linzi is humane and filial by nature, and his wit is almost that of a sage."

sentences.zh: 至於博學淵識，文章絕倫。

translations.literal: As for broad learning and deep knowledge, his writing is without peer.
translations.idiomatic: His learning runs deep and his brush has no rival."

sentences.zh: 當今天下之賢才君子，不問少長，皆願從其游而為之死，實天所以鍾福於大魏，而永授無窮之祚也。

translations.literal: The worthy gentlemen and talented men of the realm today, regardless of young or old, all wish to follow him in roaming and would die for him; truly Heaven thereby pours blessing on Great Wei and grants inexhaustible fortune forever."
translations.idiomatic: Every able man in the land, young or old, would follow him to the death—surely Heaven heaps fortune on Wei by giving us such an heir."

sentences.zh: 』欲以勸動太祖。

translations.literal: He wished thereby to stir the Grand Progenitor.
translations.idiomatic: He meant to sway Cao Cao’s heart.

sentences.zh: 太祖答曰：『植，吾愛之，安能若卿言！

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor answered, saying, "Zhi—I love him; how can he be as you say!"
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao replied: "I love Zhi—can he really be everything you claim?"

sentences.zh: 吾欲立之為嗣，何如？

translations.literal: I wish to establish him as heir—what do you think?"
translations.idiomatic: I mean to name him successor—what say you?"

sentences.zh: 』廙曰：『此國家之所以興衰，天下之所以存亡，非愚劣瑣賤者所敢與及。

translations.literal: Yì said, "This is that by which the state rises and falls, the realm survives or perishes—not something mean, foolish, petty men dare touch."
translations.idiomatic: Yì answered: "The rise and fall of the state hang on this—not a topic for small men to meddle in."

sentences.zh: 廙聞知臣莫若於君，知子莫若於父。

translations.literal: Yì has heard: none knows ministers better than the lord, none knows sons better than the father."
translations.idiomatic: Yet the proverb runs: the ruler knows his ministers best, the father his sons best."

sentences.zh: 至於君不論明闇，父不問賢愚，而能常知其臣子者何？

translations.literal: As for lord not weighing bright and dark, father not asking worthy and stupid—yet being able always to know his ministers and sons—how?"
translations.idiomatic: How then does a lord read light and shadow, or a father judge worth and folly, yet always know his men?"

sentences.zh: 蓋由相知非一事一物，相盡非一旦一夕。

translations.literal: It is because mutual knowledge is not one affair or one thing, mutual exhaustiveness is not one morning or one night."
translations.idiomatic: Because true knowledge is not won in a single glance nor sealed in a single hour."

sentences.zh: 況明公加之以聖哲，習之以人子。

translations.literal: Moreover the Illustrious Duke adds to it sage wisdom and trains him as a human son."
translations.idiomatic: You are a sage yourself and have reared him as a son."

sentences.zh: 今發明達之命，吐永安之言，可謂上應天命，下合人心，得之於須臾，垂之於萬世者也。

translations.literal: Now issuing clear-sighted commands, uttering words of lasting peace—this can be called above answering Heaven’s mandate, below joining human hearts; grasped in a moment, handed down through ten thousand generations."
translations.idiomatic: A clear edict now, a pledge of peace forever—this answers Heaven and men alike and will echo for ages."

sentences.zh: 廙不避斧鉞之誅，敢不盡言！

translations.literal: Yì does not shrink from execution by axe and halberd—how dare I not speak to the full!"
translations.idiomatic: I would face the headsman’s blade before I held back a word!"

sentences.zh: 』太祖深納之。〉

translations.literal: The Grand Progenitor deeply accepted it.〉
translations.idiomatic: Cao Cao took his counsel to heart.〉

sentences.zh: 植與諸侯並就國。

translations.literal: Zhi together with the feudal lords proceeded to their states.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi went out to his fief with the other princes.

sentences.zh: 黃初二年，監國謁者灌均希指，奏『植醉酒悖慢，劫脅使者』。

translations.literal: In the second year of Huangchu, the overseer of the princes’ domains, Herald Guan Jun, reading intent, memorialized that "Zhi, drunk, was rebellious and arrogant and coerced the envoy."
translations.idiomatic: In 221 the court watcher Guan Jun, eager to please, reported that Zhi had insulted an imperial messenger while drunk.

sentences.zh: 有司請治罪，帝以太后故，貶爵安鄉侯。

translations.literal: The responsible officials requested punishment; the Emperor, for the Empress Dowager’s sake, degraded his rank to Marquis of Anxiang.
translations.idiomatic: The ministry demanded his head; for his mother’s sake Cao Pi only stripped him to Marquis of Anxiang.

sentences.zh: 〈魏書載詔曰：『植，朕之同母弟。

translations.literal: 〈The Wei shu records an edict stating, "Zhi is my younger brother by the same mother."
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Book of Wei quotes an edict: "Zhi is my own mother’s son."

sentences.zh: 朕於天下無所不容，而況植乎？

translations.literal: I toward the realm have nothing I cannot embrace—how much more Zhi?"
translations.idiomatic: There is room in my heart for the world—shall there be none for Zhi?"

sentences.zh: 骨肉之親，舍而不誅，其改封植。』〉

translations.literal: Kin of flesh and bone—I set aside execution; change his enfeoffment for Zhi."〉
translations.idiomatic: Blood binds us; I spare his life and change his fief instead."〉

sentences.zh: 其年改封鄄城侯。

translations.literal: That year his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Juancheng.
translations.idiomatic: The same year he was made Marquis of Juancheng.

sentences.zh: 三年，立為鄄城王，邑二千五百戶。

translations.literal: In the third year, he was established as King of Juancheng, with a fief of two thousand five hundred households.
translations.idiomatic: In 222 he was raised to King of Juancheng with twenty-five hundred households.

sentences.zh: 四年，徙封雍丘王。

translations.literal: In the fourth year, his enfeoffment was transferred to King of Yongqiu.
translations.idiomatic: In 223 his seat was moved to Yongqiu.

sentences.zh: 其年，朝京都。

translations.literal: That year he attended the capital.
translations.idiomatic: That year he came to court.

sentences.zh: 上疏曰：

translations.literal: He presented a memorial, saying,
translations.idiomatic: He submitted a memorial that read:

sentences.zh: 臣自抱釁歸藩，刻肌刻骨，追思罪戾，晝分而食，夜分而寢。

translations.literal: Your subject, since bearing guilt and returning to his fief, has carved it in flesh and bone, pondering his offenses; he eats at midday division and sleeps at midnight division.
translations.idiomatic: Since I was sent back to my domain under a cloud, I have worn my guilt in my very bones—I rise at noon and retire at midnight, counting my faults.

sentences.zh: 誠以天罔不可重離，聖恩難可再恃。

translations.literal: Truly Heaven’s net may not be twice departed from; sagely favor is hard to rely on twice.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s net does not part twice for the same man, nor does imperial mercy wait on a fool forever.

sentences.zh: 竊感相鼠之篇，無禮遄死之義，形影相弔，五情愧赧。

translations.literal: Privately I am moved by the piece "Xiangshu," the meaning of "without ritual, swiftly die"; body and shadow console each other; the five emotions are ashamed and flush.
translations.idiomatic: The Ode of the Rat haunts me—"without courtesy, better die at once"—yet here stand body and shadow alone, and every passion burns with shame.

sentences.zh: 以罪棄生，則違古賢『夕改』之勸，忍活苟全，則犯詩人『胡顏』之譏。

translations.literal: To cast away life for guilt would violate the ancient worthies’ admonition to "change by evening"; to endure alive in mere preservation would incur the poets’ sneer at "what face have you."
translations.idiomatic: Die for my crimes and I spurn the sage counsel to mend at dusk; cling to life and I earn the poet’s taunt—"what cheek have you to show?"

sentences.zh: 伏惟陛下德象天地，恩隆父母，施暢春風，澤如時雨。

translations.literal: I humbly reflect that Your Majesty’s virtue images Heaven and Earth; your kindness exceeds that of parents; it spreads like the spring wind, its moisture like the timely rain.
translations.idiomatic: Your virtue spans heaven and earth; your love outdoes a father’s; it blows like spring wind and falls like seasonable rain.

sentences.zh: 是以不別荊棘者，慶雲之惠也；

translations.literal: Therefore not distinguishing thorn from bramble is the kindness of auspicious clouds;
translations.idiomatic: To spare thorn and thistle alike is the favor of the lucky cloud;

sentences.zh: 七子均養者，屍鳩之仁也；

translations.literal: to rear the seven sons equally is the humaneness of the cuckoo dove;
translations.idiomatic: to nurse seven chicks as one is the kindness of the turtle-dove;

sentences.zh: 舍罪責功者，明君之舉也；

translations.literal: to set aside blame and look to merit is the act of an enlightened lord;
translations.idiomatic: to forget fault and weigh service is the way of a wise king;

sentences.zh: 矜愚愛能者，慈父之恩也：是以愚臣徘徊於恩澤而不能自棄者也。

translations.literal: to pity folly and cherish ability is the grace of a loving father: therefore your foolish subject lingers in your kindness and cannot cast himself away."
translations.idiomatic: to pity the dull yet cherish talent is a tender father’s grace—so I hang between gratitude and despair and cannot cut myself loose."

sentences.zh: 前奉詔書，臣等絕朝，心離志絕，自分黃耇無復執珪之望。

translations.literal: Formerly receiving the edict, your subjects were cut off from court; heart departed and intent broken, I myself reckoned that in hoary old age I would never again hold the jade tablet’s hope.
translations.idiomatic: When your first order barred us from audience, I thought my heart dead and my court days over—never again to bear the jade baton.

sentences.zh: 不圖聖詔猥垂齒召，至止之日，馳心輦轂。

translations.literal: I did not expect a sagely edict humbly to descend with a summons by name; on the day I arrived, my heart raced to the imperial axle-hubs.
translations.idiomatic: I never dreamed you would stoop to call me by name; the day I reached the capital my soul flew to your chariot wheels.

sentences.zh: 僻處西館，未奉闕廷，踴躍之懷，瞻望反仄。

translations.literal: Lodging apart in the western lodge, not yet attending the palace court, the leaping in my breast looks toward it restless.
translations.idiomatic: They lodge me in the western guest hall; I have not yet seen the throne—yet my heart leaps and turns, all impatience.

sentences.zh: 謹拜表獻詩二篇，其辭曰：

translations.literal: Respectfully I bow with a table presenting two poems; their words say,
translations.idiomatic: I therefore lay before you two poems, which begin:

sentences.zh: 於穆顯考 時惟武皇

translations.literal: Oh, august was my bright-deceased father; he was Emperor Wu.
translations.idiomatic: Splendid my late father—he was Emperor Wu.

sentences.zh: 受命於天 寧濟四方

translations.literal: He received the mandate from Heaven and brought peace to the four quarters.
translations.idiomatic: He took Heaven’s charge and stilled the four seas.

sentences.zh: 朱旗所拂 九土披攘

translations.literal: Wherever the scarlet banner swept, the nine soils were laid open.
translations.idiomatic: His crimson flag swept wide; the nine domains bowed.

sentences.zh: 玄化滂流 荒服來王

translations.literal: Dark transformation poured abroad; distant lands came as kings.
translations.idiomatic: His transforming power rolled outward; wild borderlands sent kings.

sentences.zh: 超商越周 與唐比蹤

translations.literal: He surpassed Shang and Zhou; he matched the tracks of Tang.
translations.idiomatic: He outshone Shang and Zhou; he walked in Yao’s stride.

sentences.zh: 篤生我皇 奕世載聰

translations.literal: Earnestly was born my sovereign; generation after generation he bears keen wit.
translations.idiomatic: Then rose my lord—wise through the ages.

sentences.zh: 武則肅烈 文則時雍

translations.literal: In arms he is stern and fierce; in letters he is timely and harmonious.
translations.idiomatic: Terrible in war, gentle in peace.

sentences.zh: 受禪炎漢 臨君萬邦

translations.literal: He received the abdication of fiery Han and faces the myriad states as lord.
translations.idiomatic: He took the flame-red Han’s abdication and rules ten thousand lands.

sentences.zh: 萬邦既化 率由舊則

translations.literal: The myriad states transformed; all follow the ancient pattern.
translations.idiomatic: The myriad lands obey; the old statutes hold.

sentences.zh: 廣命懿親 以藩王國

translations.literal: Broadly he charged his dear kin to screen the royal domain.
translations.idiomatic: He sent kinsmen wide to fence the throne.

sentences.zh: 帝曰爾侯 君茲青土

translations.literal: The Emperor said, "You, prince—hold this green soil."
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor said: "You, my prince—this green earth is yours."

sentences.zh: 奄有海濱 方周於魯

translations.literal: You embrace the seashore; your bounds rival Zhou of Lu.
translations.idiomatic: You hold the coast; your realm rivals Lu of old.

sentences.zh: 車服有輝 旗章有敘

translations.literal: Carriages and robes shine; flags and insignia keep order.
translations.idiomatic: Bright your chariots and robes; ordered your banners and blazons.

sentences.zh: 濟濟雋乂 我弼我輔

translations.literal: In hosts the splendid talents are my buttresses, my aids.
translations.idiomatic: Hosts of fine men are my props and stays.

sentences.zh: 伊予小子 恃寵驕盈

translations.literal: I, this little child, relied on favor and swelled with pride.
translations.idiomatic: I, a foolish boy, leaned on favor and swelled proud.

sentences.zh: 舉掛時網 動亂國經

translations.literal: I snagged the net of the times and stirred the state’s warp.
translations.idiomatic: I tangled in the age’s net and snapped the kingdom’s cord.

sentences.zh: 作藩作屏 先軌是墮

translations.literal: Made screen and shield, I let the former track fall.
translations.idiomatic: You made me a shield—I broke the ancient rule.

sentences.zh: 傲我皇使 犯我朝儀

translations.literal: I insulted the imperial envoy and violated court ritual.
translations.idiomatic: I slighted your herald and mocked the court’s rite.

sentences.zh: 國有典刑 我削我絀

translations.literal: The state has its statutes; I was cut, I was stripped.
translations.idiomatic: The law has teeth—I was shorn and cast down.

sentences.zh: 將寘於理 元凶是率

translations.literal: They would have set me before the judge; I led the chief culprit’s part.
translations.idiomatic: They would have bound me to justice—I was ringleader of the wrong.

sentences.zh: 明明天子 時篤同類

translations.literal: Bright, bright the Son of Heaven—at this time he cherishes those of his kind deeply.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s Son, clear of eye—holds his kindred dear.

sentences.zh: 不忍我刑 暴之朝肆

translations.literal: He could not bear my punishment; he would not expose me in the morning market.
translations.idiomatic: He would not shame me on the public block.

sentences.zh: 違彼執憲 哀予小子

translations.literal: Turning from those who hold the law, he pitied me, the little child.
translations.idiomatic: He set the judge aside and pitied this small son.

sentences.zh: 改封兗邑 於河之濱

translations.literal: He changed my fief to Yan territory, by the river’s shore.
translations.idiomatic: He moved my seat to Yan, beside the river’s brim.

sentences.zh: 股肱弗置 有君無臣

translations.literal: Arms and legs were not set in place—there was a lord, no ministers.
translations.idiomatic: No helpers at my side—only a lord, no ministers.

sentences.zh: 荒淫之闕 誰弼予身

translations.literal: In the fault of wanton excess, who would brace my person?
translations.idiomatic: Lost in license and sloth, who would brace my frame?

sentences.zh: 煢煢僕夫 於彼冀方

translations.literal: Alone, alone, my groom—there in the Ji region.
translations.idiomatic: Lonely my groom and I—far off in Ji.

sentences.zh: 嗟予小子 乃罹斯殃

translations.literal: Alas, I, the little child—thus I met this disaster.
translations.idiomatic: Alas, this boy—such ruin fell on me.

sentences.zh: 赫赫天子 恩不遺物

translations.literal: Radiant, radiant the Son of Heaven—his grace leaves nothing out.
translations.idiomatic: Bright Heaven’s Son—his grace spares nothing.

sentences.zh: 冠我玄冕 要我朱紱

translations.literal: He set on me the dark crown, bound on me the vermillion sash.
translations.idiomatic: He crowned me in black silk, tied the crimson cord.

sentences.zh: 朱紱光大 使我榮華

translations.literal: The vermillion sash shines great—he made me glorious.
translations.idiomatic: The crimson cord gleams wide—he gave me glory.

sentences.zh: 剖符授玉 王爵是加

translations.literal: He split the tally, handed the jade—kingly rank was added.
translations.idiomatic: He halved the tally, gave the jade—raised me to prince.

sentences.zh: 仰齒金璽 俯執聖策

translations.literal: I look up to bite the golden seal; I bow to grasp the sacred writ.
translations.idiomatic: I lift the golden seal; I bow and take the sacred writ.

sentences.zh: 皇恩過隆 祗承怵惕

translations.literal: Imperial favor passes measure—I receive it trembling.
translations.idiomatic: The favor is too high—I take it in fear.

sentences.zh: 咨我小子 頑凶是嬰

translations.literal: Ah, me, the little child—stubborn evil wraps me round.
translations.idiomatic: Woe, this stubborn child—evil clings like a swaddling band.

sentences.zh: 逝慚陵墓 存愧闕廷

translations.literal: Dead, I shame the tombs; living, I shame the palace court.
