translations.idiomatic: Dead I shame the tombs; alive I shame your hall.

sentences.zh: 匪敢傲德 實恩是恃

translations.literal: I dare not flout virtue—I lean on favor alone.
translations.idiomatic: I dare not scorn your virtue—I cling to mercy alone.

sentences.zh: 威靈改加 足以沒齒

translations.literal: Majestic power changed toward me—enough to hide my teeth to the grave.
translations.idiomatic: Your aweful grace remade me—enough to hide my shame till the grave.

sentences.zh: 昊天罔極 性命不圖

translations.literal: High Heaven has no limit—life and fate lie not in my plan.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s height knows no bound—my life is not my own to chart.

sentences.zh: 常懼顛沛 抱罪黃壚

translations.literal: I ever fear overturn and bear guilt to the yellow springs.
translations.idiomatic: I dread a fall that drags my guilt down to the yellow springs.

sentences.zh: 願蒙矢石 建旗東嶽

translations.literal: I wish to meet stone and arrow, to raise a banner on the eastern peak.
translations.idiomatic: I would meet stone and shaft and plant your flag on Taishan’s height.

sentences.zh: 庶立豪氂 微功自贖

translations.literal: Perhaps to set up a hair’s weight of merit and redeem myself in small measure.
translations.idiomatic: Perhaps earn a hair’s weight of merit to buy off my fault.

sentences.zh: 危軀授命 知足免戾

translations.literal: Risk this body, give life—content if it clears my guilt.
translations.idiomatic: Give this frail life gladly—if guilt lifts, I am content.

sentences.zh: 甘赴江湘 奮戈吳越

translations.literal: Gladly I would haste to the Yangzi and Xiang, shake spear in Wu and Yue.
translations.idiomatic: I would march to the Yangzi’s waves and strike for you in Wu and Yue.

sentences.zh: 天啟其衷 得會京畿

translations.literal: Heaven opened his inmost heart; I was allowed to meet the capital region.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven relented; I may see the capital again.

sentences.zh: 遲奉聖顏 如渴如飢

translations.literal: Tardily I attend the sagely countenance—as thirst, as hunger.
translations.idiomatic: Slowly I near your face—as parched men crave rain, as the starving crave bread.

sentences.zh: 心之雲慕 愴矣其悲

translations.literal: The heart’s cloud of longing—how bitter, how sad.
translations.idiomatic: My heart is a cloud of longing—grief without end.

sentences.zh: 天高聽卑 皇肯照微

translations.literal: Heaven is high yet hears the lowly; will my sovereign deign to shine on this least subject?
translations.idiomatic: High Heaven hears the humble—will you, my emperor, light even me?

sentences.zh: 又曰：

translations.literal: It also says,
translations.idiomatic: A second poem says:

sentences.zh: 肅承明詔 應會皇都

translations.literal: Reverently I take the lucid edict and answer the summons to the royal capital.
translations.idiomatic: I bow to your clear command and hasten to the capital.

sentences.zh: 星陳夙駕 秣馬脂車

translations.literal: Like stars arrayed I rise before dawn, feed the horses and grease the chariot.
translations.idiomatic: Before dawn I harness, grain the horses, oil the axles.

sentences.zh: 命彼掌徒 肅我征旅

translations.literal: I bid the overseer of my train to marshal my marching men.
translations.idiomatic: I order my stewards to set my escort in order.

sentences.zh: 朝發鸞台 夕宿蘭渚

translations.literal: At dawn I leave the phoenix terrace; at dusk I lodge on orchid isle.
translations.idiomatic: We quit the tower at dawn and make orchid shoals by nightfall.

sentences.zh: 芒芒原隰 祁祁士女

translations.literal: Vast the moors and marshes; thick the folk along the road.
translations.idiomatic: Endless moors, crowds of travelers on every hand.

sentences.zh: 經彼公田 樂我稷黍

translations.literal: We pass the lord’s fields and joy in the millet and grain.
translations.idiomatic: We cross the public fields and feast our eyes on the crops.

sentences.zh: 爰有樛木 重陰匪息

translations.literal: There stands a twisted tree; layered shade gives no rest.
translations.idiomatic: A stooping tree spreads shade where we cannot linger.

sentences.zh: 雖有餱糧 飢不遑食

translations.literal: Though we carry dry rations, hunger leaves no time to eat.
translations.idiomatic: Though we pack provisions, hunger will not let us pause to eat.

sentences.zh: 望城不過 面邑匪游

translations.literal: We sight walled towns yet do not enter; we face boroughs yet do not roam.
translations.idiomatic: We pass cities without stopping, skirt towns without tarrying.

sentences.zh: 僕夫警策 平路是由

translations.literal: The groom snaps his whip; the level road is the path we take.
translations.idiomatic: The driver lays on the whip; we hold to the straight highway.

sentences.zh: 玄駟藹藹 揚鑣漂沫

translations.literal: The black four-horse team moves stately; bridles lift, foam flies.
translations.idiomatic: The jet team rolls on, bits high, froth flying.

sentences.zh: 流風翼衡 輕雲承蓋

translations.literal: Wind streams like wings along the yoke; thin clouds bear up the canopy.
translations.idiomatic: Wind fans the crossbar like wings; light clouds bear the carriage hood.

sentences.zh: 涉澗之濱 緣山之隈

translations.literal: We ford the stream’s brink and hug the mountain’s curve.
translations.idiomatic: We cross the ford and trace the mountain’s bend.

sentences.zh: 遵彼河滸 黃阪是階

translations.literal: We follow the river’s bank; the yellow slope is our stair.
translations.idiomatic: We keep to the river road; the yellow ridge is our climb.

sentences.zh: 西濟關谷 或降或升

translations.literal: Westward we cross passes and gorges, now down, now up.
translations.idiomatic: West through the passes we climb and descend by turns.

sentences.zh: 騑驂倦路 再寢再興

translations.literal: The outriders and traces grow weary on the road; we sleep and rise again.
translations.idiomatic: Trace-horses tire on the long road; we sleep, wake, and press on.

sentences.zh: 將朝聖皇 匪敢晏寧

translations.literal: I am bound for the sage emperor—I dare not tarry in ease.
translations.idiomatic: I ride to my sovereign—I dare not seek comfort.

sentences.zh: 弭節長騖 指日遄徵

translations.literal: I slack rein only to gallop far; I count the days of swift march.
translations.idiomatic: I check the bit only to race on; each sun marks a day nearer you.

sentences.zh: 前驅舉燧 後乘抗旌

translations.literal: The van raises beacon fires; the rear guard lifts long banners.
translations.idiomatic: Vanguard lights the signal fires; rearguard flies the great flags.

sentences.zh: 輪不輟運 鸞無廢聲

translations.literal: Wheels never cease their turning; phoenix bells never lose their tone.
translations.idiomatic: The wheels never stop; the carriage bells never fall silent.

sentences.zh: 爰暨帝室 稅此西墉

translations.literal: Thus I reach the imperial precincts and alight at this western wall.
translations.idiomatic: At last I reach the palace and dismount at the western lodging.

sentences.zh: 嘉詔未賜 朝覲莫從

translations.literal: The gracious edict has not yet allowed audience; I may not yet attend court.
translations.idiomatic: Your kind summons has not yet let me enter; I cannot yet bow in the hall.

sentences.zh: 仰瞻城閾 俯惟闕廷

translations.literal: I look up at the gate towers; I look down and think on the palace court.
translations.idiomatic: I lift my eyes to the gate towers; I bow my head and ache for the throne room.

sentences.zh: 長懷永慕 憂心如酲

translations.literal: Longing without end, my grief is like the morning after wine.
translations.idiomatic: Endless longing racks me like a wine-sickness in the heart.

sentences.zh: 六年，帝東征，還過雍丘，幸植宮，增戶五百。

translations.literal: In the sixth year, the Emperor campaigned east; returning he passed Yongqiu, visited Zhi’s palace, and increased his households by five hundred.
translations.idiomatic: In 225 the emperor marched east; on his return he stopped at Yongqiu, visited Zhi’s residence, and added five hundred households to his fief.

sentences.zh: 太和元年，徙封浚儀。

translations.literal: In the first year of Taihe, his enfeoffment was transferred to Junyi.
translations.idiomatic: In 227 he was moved to Junyi.

sentences.zh: 二年，復還雍丘。

translations.literal: In the second year, he was returned again to Yongqiu.
translations.idiomatic: In 228 he was sent back to Yongqiu.

sentences.zh: 植常自憤怨，抱利器而無所施，上疏求自試曰：

translations.literal: Zhi often harbored resentment in himself, embracing sharp tools yet having nowhere to apply them; he presented a memorial begging to be tried, saying,
translations.idiomatic: Zhi nursed a steady anger: he had a sword’s edge and no wall to try it on. He submitted a memorial asking for a chance to prove himself:

sentences.zh: 臣聞士之生世，入則事父，出則事君；

translations.literal: Your subject has heard that a gentleman born into the world, within serves his father, without serves his lord;
translations.idiomatic: I have heard that a man born to this age serves his father at home and his prince abroad;

sentences.zh: 事父尚於榮親，事君貴於興國。

translations.literal: serving the father values bringing honor to kin; serving the lord values raising the state to glory.
translations.idiomatic: the son’s duty is to bring glory to his kin; the minister’s duty is to exalt his sovereign’s house.

sentences.zh: 故慈父不能愛無益之子，仁君不能畜無用之臣。

translations.literal: Therefore a loving father cannot cherish a useless son, nor a humane lord keep a useless minister.
translations.idiomatic: So no loving father dotes on a worthless son, and no humane king feeds a useless officer.

sentences.zh: 夫論德而授官者，成功之君也；

translations.literal: He who weighs virtue and then grants office is a lord who completes his work;
translations.idiomatic: The king who matches rank to character finishes his great work;

sentences.zh: 量能而受爵者，畢命之臣也。

translations.literal: he who measures capacity and then bestows noble rank is a minister who exhausts his life in service.
translations.idiomatic: the servant who takes title only as his talent allows gives his life to the end.

sentences.zh: 故君無虛授，臣無虛受；

translations.literal: Therefore the lord grants no empty title, the minister accepts no empty salary;
translations.idiomatic: Thus no crown sits idle on a head, no stipend fills an empty hand;

sentences.zh: 虛授謂之謬舉，虛受謂之屍祿，詩之『素餐』所由作也。

translations.literal: empty grant is called a mistaken appointment; empty acceptance is called corpse-salary—this is why the Odes speak of “eating white rice.”
translations.idiomatic: a hollow title is a false choice; pay for no work is “corpse on the payroll”—the shame the Odes call “eating free grain.”

sentences.zh: 昔二虢不辭兩國之任，其德厚也；

translations.literal: Formerly the two Guo did not decline the burden of two states—their virtue was thick.
translations.idiomatic: The two Guo brothers did not shun twin duties—their virtue ran deep.

sentences.zh: 旦、奭不讓燕、魯之封，其功大也。

translations.literal: Dan and Shi did not yield the enfeoffments of Yan and Lu—their merit was great.
translations.idiomatic: The Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao did not refuse Yan and Lu—their merit was vast.

sentences.zh: 今臣蒙國重恩，三世於今矣。

translations.literal: Now your subject has received the state’s deep favor; three generations down to today.
translations.idiomatic: I have drunk deep of the dynasty’s kindness—three generations of my house.

sentences.zh: 正值陛下升平之際，沐浴聖澤，潛潤德教，可謂厚幸矣。

translations.literal: Just as I meet Your Majesty’s age of peace, I bathe in sagely moisture and silently soak in virtuous teaching—this may be called great good fortune.
translations.idiomatic: I live under your peace, washed in holy dew and steeped in your teaching—no man could be luckier.

sentences.zh: 而竊位東藩，爵在上列，身被輕暖，口厭百味，目極華靡，耳倦絲竹者，爵重祿厚之所致也。

translations.literal: Yet I steal a place as eastern bulwark, my noble rank among the highest ranks; my body is wrapped in light furs, my mouth surfeits on a hundred flavors, my eyes reach the utmost splendor, my ears weary of strings and pipes—this is what weighty rank and thick salary have brought.
translations.idiomatic: Yet I hold a princedom in the east, rank among the first, dress in silken furs, dine on every delicacy, feast my eyes on luxury, tire my ears with music—all because my title is high and my pay rich.

sentences.zh: 退念古之授爵祿者，有異於此，皆以功勤濟國，輔主惠民。

translations.literal: Stepping back, I reflect that those of old who received noble rank and salary differed from this: all by merit and toil saved the state, aided the lord, and benefited the people.
translations.idiomatic: Looking back, the men of old who took stipend earned it—by sweat they saved the state, steadied the throne, and fed the people.

sentences.zh: 今臣無德可述，無功可紀，若此終年無益國朝，將掛風人『彼其』之譏。

translations.literal: Now your subject has no virtue to relate, no merit to record; if in this way year after year I benefit not the court, I shall hang the poet’s sneer of “what are they like?”
translations.idiomatic: I have no tale of virtue, no scroll of deeds; if I rot here year on year, I earn the poet’s gibe at useless lords.

sentences.zh: 是以上慚玄冕，俯愧朱紱。

translations.literal: Therefore above I shame the dark crown, below I blush at the vermillion sash.
translations.idiomatic: So I blush for the black cap above me and the crimson cord at my waist.

sentences.zh: 方今天下一統，九州晏如，而顧西有違命之蜀，東有不臣之吳，使邊境未得脫甲，謀士未得高枕者，誠欲混同宇內以致太和也。

translations.literal: Now the realm is unified, the nine provinces tranquil—yet to the west there is Shu that defies your command, to the east Wu that will not acknowledge fealty, so that the borders cannot lay down armor nor strategists sleep on high pillows; truly it is because you desire to merge the realm within the four seas and bring about Great Harmony.
translations.idiomatic: The empire is one and the nine regions calm—yet Shu in the west and Wu in the east still hold aloof, so our spears stay bright and our planners cannot sleep—because you mean to unite all under heaven in perfect peace.

sentences.zh: 故啟滅有扈而夏功昭，成克商、奄而周德著。

translations.literal: Therefore when Qi smote Youhu, Xia’s merit shone; when Cheng overcame Shang and the Yan remnant, Zhou’s virtue stood clear.
translations.idiomatic: So Qi crushed Youhu and Xia’s glory blazed; King Cheng conquered Shang and the loyalist state of Yan and Zhou’s power was plain.

sentences.zh: 今陛下以聖明統世，將欲卒文、武之功，繼成、康之隆，簡賢授能，以方叔、召虎之臣鎮御四境，為國爪牙者，可謂當矣。

translations.literal: Now Your Majesty, with sagely brilliance ruling the age, will complete the work of Wen and Wu, continue the height of Cheng and Kang, select the worthy and assign the able, and with ministers like Fangshu and Zhaohu guard the four quarters as the state’s claws and fangs—this can be called fitting.
translations.idiomatic: You, sage king, mean to finish what Wen and Wu began, match Cheng and Kang, pick able men, and with Fangshu and Zhaohu’s like hold the frontiers as the kingdom’s claws—none could call that wrong.

sentences.zh: 然而高鳥未掛於輕繳，淵魚未縣於鉤餌者，恐釣射之術或未盡也。

translations.literal: Yet the high bird is not yet caught on a light cord, nor the deep fish hung on hook and bait—I fear the arts of angling and shooting are not yet exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: Yet the lofty bird is not snared nor the deep fish hooked—the hunter’s and angler’s craft may still need polish.

sentences.zh: 昔耿弇不俟光武，亟擊張步，言不以賊遺於君父。

translations.literal: Formerly Geng Yan did not await Guangwu but urgently struck Zhang Bu, saying he would not leave the bandit to his lord and father.
translations.idiomatic: Geng Yan would not wait for Guangwu but struck Zhang Bu at once, saying he would not leave the bandit for his sovereign and sire.

sentences.zh: 故車右伏劍於鳴轂，雍門刎首於齊境，若此二士，豈惡生而尚死哉？

translations.literal: Therefore the chariot-right drew his sword at the rumbling axle-hub, and Yongmen cut his throat in Qi’s territory—were these two gentlemen ones who hated life and honored death?
translations.idiomatic: So the chariot guard bared steel at a rattling wheel, and Yongmen Di cut his throat in Qi—did those men love death for its own sake?

sentences.zh: 誠忿其慢主而陵君也。

translations.literal: Truly they resented those who slighted their lord and insulted their sovereign.
translations.idiomatic: They could not bear insult to their king.

sentences.zh: 〈劉向說苑曰：越甲至齊，雍門狄請死之。

translations.literal: 〈Liu Xiang’s Shuoyuan states: Yue armor reached Qi, and Yongmen Di begged to die for it.
translations.idiomatic: 〈Liu Xiang’s Garden of Stories: when Yue’s army reached Qi, Yongmen Di asked leave to die for his state.

sentences.zh: 齊王曰：『鼓鐸之聲未聞，矢石未交，長兵未接，子何務死？

translations.literal: The king of Qi said, “The drums and bells have not been heard, stones and arrows have not crossed, long weapons have not met—why are you bent on death?
translations.idiomatic: The king said: “No drum has sounded, no shaft has flown—why rush to die?

sentences.zh: 知為人臣之禮邪？

translations.literal: Do you know the ritual of serving as minister?”
translations.idiomatic: Do you know what it is to serve a prince?”

sentences.zh: 』雍門狄對曰：『臣聞之，昔者王田於囿，左轂鳴，車右請死之，王曰：「子何為死？

translations.literal: Yongmen Di replied, “Your subject has heard: of old the king hunted in the park; the left hub-rim rang; the chariot-right asked to die for it; the king said, ‘Why would you die for this?’
translations.idiomatic: Yongmen Di answered: “They say the king once hunted in the park; the left wheel-hub creaked; the chariot guard asked to die; the king asked, ‘Why die for that?’

sentences.zh: 」車右曰：「為其鳴吾君也。

translations.literal: The chariot-right said, ‘It is because it has shamed my lord.’
translations.idiomatic: The guard said, ‘Because it has dishonored you.’

sentences.zh: 」王曰：「左轂鳴者，此工師之罪也。

translations.literal: The king said, ‘The left hub’s ringing is the workmen’s fault.’
translations.idiomatic: The king said, ‘That squeak is the coachwright’s fault.’

sentences.zh: 子何事之有焉？

translations.literal: What affair is it of yours?”
translations.idiomatic: What is that to you?”

sentences.zh: 」車右對曰：「吾不見工師之乘，而見其鳴吾君也。

translations.literal: The chariot-right replied, ‘I have not seen the workmen’s chariot, but I have seen it shame my lord.’
translations.idiomatic: The guard replied, ‘I have not seen the workmen’s cart; I have seen my lord shamed.’

sentences.zh: 」遂刎頸而死。

translations.literal: Thereupon he cut his throat and died.
translations.idiomatic: He cut his own throat and died.

sentences.zh: 有是乎？

translations.literal: Was there such a thing?”
translations.idiomatic: Did that truly happen?”

sentences.zh: 』王曰：『有之。

translations.literal: The king said, “There was.”
translations.idiomatic: The king said, “It did.”

sentences.zh: 』雍門狄曰：『今越甲至，其鳴吾君，豈左轂之下哉？

translations.literal: Yongmen Di said, “Now Yue’s armor has come; it shames my lord—is it less than a left hub’s squeak?
translations.idiomatic: Yongmen Di said: “Yue’s host is here—it shames you worse than a wheel’s creak.

sentences.zh: 車右可以死左轂，而臣獨不可以死越甲邪？

translations.literal: The chariot-right may die for the left hub—how can your subject alone not die for Yue’s armor?”
translations.idiomatic: The guard could die for a hub—may I not die for Yue?”

sentences.zh: 』遂刎頸而死。

translations.literal: Thereupon he cut his throat and died.
translations.idiomatic: He cut his throat and fell dead.

sentences.zh: 是日，越人引軍而退七十里，曰：『齊王有臣，鈞如雍門狄，疑使越社稷不血食。

translations.literal: That day the men of Yue led their army back seventy li, saying, “The king of Qi has a subject equal to Yongmen Di—we fear Yue’s altars will receive no blood sacrifice.”
translations.idiomatic: That day the Yue army withdrew seventy li, saying, “If Qi has men like Yongmen Di, our state may starve.”

sentences.zh: 』遂歸。

translations.literal: Thereupon they returned.
translations.idiomatic: So they marched home.

sentences.zh: 齊王葬雍門狄以上卿之禮。〉

translations.literal: The king of Qi buried Yongmen Di with the rites of a senior minister.〉
translations.idiomatic: The king of Qi buried Yongmen Di with honors fit for a high minister.〉

sentences.zh: 夫君之寵臣，欲以除患興利；

translations.literal: Now the lord’s favored ministers desire thereby to remove harm and raise profit;
translations.idiomatic: A king cherishes good servants to scourge foes and build the realm;

sentences.zh: 臣之事君，必以殺身靖亂，以功報主也。

translations.literal: the minister’s service to his lord must be to give his body to still rebellion and repay the lord with merit.
translations.idiomatic: a minister’s trade is to hazard life, crush revolt, and pay his debt in deeds.

sentences.zh: 昔賈誼弱冠，求試屬國，請系單於之頸而制其命；

translations.literal: Formerly Jia Yi, still in his cap’s first year, begged trial as chief of dependent states and asked to tie the Chanyu’s neck and control his life;
translations.idiomatic: Jia Yi at twenty asked for a border post and swore he would rope the Chanyu’s neck;

sentences.zh: 終軍以妙年使越，欲得長纓纓其王，羈致北闕。

translations.literal: Zhong Jun, in the flower of youth, was sent to Yue and wished to take a long cord to halter its king and drag him to the northern gate.
translations.idiomatic: Zhong Jun, barely grown, went south and vowed to lead the king of Yue bound to Chang’an.

sentences.zh: 此二臣，豈好為誇主而耀世哉？

translations.literal: Could these two ministers have loved to boast before their lord and dazzle the age?
translations.idiomatic: Those two were not bragging for fame.

sentences.zh: 志或鬱結，欲逞其才力，輸能於明君也。

translations.literal: Their aims were pent up; they wished to display their strength and pour their ability before an enlightened lord.
translations.idiomatic: Their hearts were pent; they longed to lay their power before a wise throne.

sentences.zh: 昔漢武為霍去病治第，辭曰：『匈奴未滅，臣無以家為！』

translations.literal: Formerly Han Wudi built a mansion for Huo Qubing, who declined, saying, “The Xiongnu are not yet destroyed—your servant has no home to speak of!”
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wu built Huo Qubing a palace, he answered: “While the Xiongnu live, I have no home.”

translations.literal: 〈Gu〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈Some editions read gu “indeed” here.〉

sentences.zh: 夫憂國忘家，捐軀濟難，忠臣之志也。

translations.literal: To worry for the state and forget one’s house, to cast aside the body to save peril—this is the mind of a loyal minister.
translations.idiomatic: To fret for the realm and forget hearth, to stake life on danger—that is a loyal heart.

sentences.zh: 今臣居外，非不厚也，而寢不安席，食不遑味者，伏以二方未克為念。

translations.literal: Now your subject dwells abroad—not without comfort—yet cannot rest easy on his mat nor taste his food’s flavor, because he broods on the two regions not yet conquered.
translations.idiomatic: I live abroad in no small comfort—yet I cannot sleep or savor my meat, for Shu and Wu still stand.

sentences.zh: 伏見先武皇帝武臣宿將，年耆即世者有聞矣。

translations.literal: I humbly observe that among Emperor Wu’s martial ministers and veteran generals, word comes that those grown old have passed from the world.
translations.idiomatic: I note that Wu’s old captains are dying off with the years.

sentences.zh: 雖賢不乏世，宿將舊卒，猶習戰陳，竊不自量，志在效命，庶立毛髮之功，以報所受之恩。

translations.literal: Though worthies are not lacking in the age, seasoned generals and old soldiers still are practiced in battle formations; I privately do not measure myself, but my intent is to offer my life, hoping to set up merit the weight of a hair and repay the grace I have received.
translations.idiomatic: Young men still come forward, and the ranks remember war; I dare not flatter myself, yet I would spend my life for a hair’s worth of merit to repay your kindness.

sentences.zh: 若使陛下出不世之詔，效臣錐刀之用，使得西屬大將軍，當一校之隊，若東屬大司馬，統偏舟之任，必乘危蹈險，騁舟奮驪，突刃觸鋒，為士卒先。

translations.literal: If Your Majesty would issue an edict unmatched in the age and employ your servant’s blade’s edge, letting me attach to the west under the Grand General and lead one cohort’s column, or attach to the east under the Grand Marshal and command a flotilla’s duty—I would surely ride danger and tread peril, gallop boats and lash swift steeds, crash blades and meet points, and go ahead of the soldiers.
translations.idiomatic: If you would send a matchless call and use this poor blade—let me serve under the Grand General in the west with one column, or under the Grand Marshal in the east with a squadron—I would face every risk, drive the fleet, spur the horses, and lead the charge.

sentences.zh: 雖未能禽權馘亮，庶將虜其雄率，殲其醜類，必效須臾之捷，以滅終身之愧，使名掛史筆，事列朝策。

translations.literal: Though I may not capture Quan and behead Liang, I hope at least to seize their chief commanders, wipe out their vile host, surely achieve a moment’s swift victory, and blot out a lifetime’s shame, so that my name hangs on the historian’s brush and my deeds are listed in the court’s plans.
translations.idiomatic: I may not nail Sun Quan nor take Zhuge Liang’s head, yet I would crush their champions, scour their rabble, win one swift hour, and wash away my shame—so history records my name and the court files my deed.

sentences.zh: 雖身分蜀境，首縣吳闕，猶生之年也。

translations.literal: Though my body be cut off in Shu’s borders, my head hung at Wu’s gate, it would still be life to me.
translations.idiomatic: If my body falls in Shu and my head adorns a Wu gate-post, I would count myself alive.

sentences.zh: 如微才弗試，沒世無聞，徒榮其軀而豐其體，生無益於事，死無損於數，虛荷上位而忝重祿，禽息鳥視，終於白首，此徒圈牢之養物，非臣之所志也。

translations.literal: If my slight talent is not tried and I pass from the world unknown, vainly fattening my frame and enriching my flesh—living without profit to affairs, dying without harm to the tally—then I bear empty rank and disgrace thick salary, peck and stare like birds until white-haired end: this is merely the raising of pen-stock creatures; it is not your servant’s intent.
translations.idiomatic: If you never test me and I die unheard, a fattened beast in a pen—useless alive, unmourned dead—then I am only fodder for the cage, not the servant you need.

sentences.zh: 流聞東軍失備，師徒小衄，輟食棄餐，奮袂攘衽，撫劍東顧，而心已馳於吳會矣。

translations.literal: Rumor tells me the eastern army lost its readiness and the troops suffered a small check; I stopped eating, cast aside my meal, flung back my sleeves, clutched my sword, looked east, and my heart had already galloped to Wu and Guiji.
translations.idiomatic: Word says the eastern host was caught unprepared and took a small wound—I dropped my bowl, seized my sword, and my soul was already racing toward Wu.

sentences.zh: 臣昔從先武皇帝南極赤岸，東臨滄海，西望玉門，北出玄塞，伏見所以行軍用兵之勢，可謂神妙矣。

translations.literal: Your subject formerly followed Emperor Wu south to Red Shore, east to face the deep sea, west to gaze on Jade Gate, north out through Dark Pass—I humbly observed how he marched armies and used troops; it can be called divine and subtle.
translations.idiomatic: I once rode with Emperor Wu south to Red Shore, east to the sea, west to Jade Gate, north through Dark Pass—I saw how he moved armies: it was sorcery.

sentences.zh: 故兵者不可豫言，臨難而制變者也。

translations.literal: Therefore war cannot be spoken of beforehand; facing peril, one makes changes.
translations.idiomatic: War admits no rehearsal; you remake the plan when steel meets steel.

sentences.zh: 志欲自效於明時，立功於聖世。

translations.literal: My intent is to offer myself in this enlightened age and set up merit in this sagely generation.
translations.idiomatic: I mean to give myself to this age and carve one mark on your reign.

sentences.zh: 每覽史籍，觀古忠臣義士，出一朝之命，以徇國家之難，身雖屠裂，而功銘著於鼎鍾，名稱垂於竹帛，未嘗不拊心而嘆息也。

translations.literal: Whenever I peruse the histories and observe the ancient loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen who staked a court’s life to follow the state through disaster—though their bodies were hacked apart, their merit was inscribed on the tripods and bells, their names hang down on bamboo and silk—never have I failed to strike my breast and sigh.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I read how loyal men staked all for the state—torn limb from limb yet named on bronze and silk—I beat my breast and sigh.

sentences.zh: 臣聞明主使臣，不廢有罪。

translations.literal: Your subject has heard that the enlightened lord employs ministers and does not discard the guilty.
translations.idiomatic: I have heard wise kings use even broken men.

sentences.zh: 故奔北敗軍之將用，秦、魯以成其功；

translations.literal: Therefore generals who fled defeat were employed, and Qin and Lu thereby completed their work;
translations.idiomatic: Routed generals found work again, and Qin and Lu reaped the gain;

sentences.zh: 〈臣松之案：秦用敗軍之將，事顯，故不註。

translations.literal: 〈Your subject Pei Songzhi notes: Qin’s use of defeated generals is well known, so I do not annotate.
translations.idiomatic: 〈Pei Songzhi: Qin’s use of fallen commanders is famous, so I skip it.

sentences.zh: 魯連與燕將書曰：『曹子為魯將，三戰三北而亡地五百裡，向使曹子計不反顧，義不旋踵，刎頸而死，則亦不免為敗軍之將矣。

translations.literal: Lu Lian’s letter to the Yan general states, “Cao Mo served Lu as general, fought three battles, fled three times, and lost five hundred li of land; had Cao Mo then resolved never to turn his head and, on principle, not swivel his heel, cut his throat and died, he would still have been no more than a defeated general.”
translations.idiomatic: Lu Lian wrote the Yan general: “Cao Mo led Lu’s army, lost three fights and five hundred li of ground; had he then killed himself for shame, he would still be remembered only as a beaten general.”

sentences.zh: 曹子棄三北之恥，而退與魯君計。

translations.literal: Cao Mo cast aside the shame of three defeats and withdrew to take counsel with the lord of Lu.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Mo swallowed the shame of three routs and went home to plan with his duke.

sentences.zh: 桓公朝天子，會諸侯，曹子以一劍之任，披桓公之心於壇坫之上，顏色不變，辭氣不悖。

translations.literal: Duke Huan attended the Son of Heaven and met the feudal lords; Cao Mo, with the duty of one sword, laid bare Duke Huan’s breast on the altar of alliance—his color did not change, his words showed no disorder.
translations.idiomatic: When Duke Huan met the Son of Heaven and the lords, Cao Mo with a single blade bared Huan’s chest on the covenant mound—never blinking, never stumbling in speech.

sentences.zh: 三戰之所亡，一朝而復之。

translations.literal: What three battles had lost, in one morning he recovered.
translations.idiomatic: In one morning he won back all that three defeats had cost.

sentences.zh: 天下震動，諸侯驚駭，威加吳、越。

translations.literal: The realm trembled; the feudal lords were awestruck; his might reached Wu and Yue.
translations.idiomatic: The world shook; the lords gaped; his name rolled as far as Wu and Yue.

sentences.zh: 』若此二士者，非不能成小廉而行小節也。〉

translations.literal: Men like these two were not unable to practice petty integrity and walk in petty bounds.〉
translations.idiomatic: Those men were not too small for scruple—they simply aimed higher.〉

sentences.zh: 絕纓盜馬之臣赦，楚、趙以濟其難。

translations.literal: The ministers who snapped the cap-tassel and stole horses were pardoned, and Chu and Zhao thereby passed through their peril.
translations.idiomatic: Chu forgave the man who snatched his tassel; Zhao spared the groom who stole horses—both kingdoms were saved by mercy.

sentences.zh: 〈臣松之案：楚莊掩絕纓之罪，事亦顯，故不書。

translations.literal: 〈Your subject Pei Songzhi notes: King Zhuang of Chu’s covering the offense of the snapped tassel is also well known, so I do not record it.
translations.idiomatic: 〈Pei Songzhi: Zhuang of Chu’s “snapped tassel” story is famous, so I omit it here.

sentences.zh: 秦穆公有赦盜馬事，趙則未聞。

translations.literal: Duke Mu of Qin had the incident of pardoning horse-thieves; as for Zhao I have not heard of one.
translations.idiomatic: Duke Mu of Qin pardoned horse-thieves; I find no Zhao parallel.

sentences.zh: 蓋以秦亦趙姓，故互文以避上『秦』字也。〉

translations.literal: Probably because Qin also shares the Zhao surname, the text uses mutual phrasing to avoid repeating the graph “Qin” above.〉
translations.idiomatic: The text pairs “Chu and Zhao” because Qin was of Zhao lineage—scribal avoidance of repeating “Qin.”〉

sentences.zh: 臣竊感先帝早崩，威王棄世，臣獨何人，以堪長久！

translations.literal: Your subject privately grieves that the late emperor departed early, Prince Weishu abandoned the world—what manner of man am I, that I could long endure!
translations.idiomatic: The late emperor died young, my brother Cao Zhang gone too—what am I, that I should outlive them?

sentences.zh: 常恐先朝露，填溝壑，墳土未乾，而身名並滅。

translations.literal: I constantly fear to precede the morning dew, fill ditches and gullies, and before the grave’s earth is dry both body and name be extinguished.
translations.idiomatic: I dread I will vanish like dew, fill an anonymous ditch, and leave no name while my tomb is still fresh.

sentences.zh: 臣聞騏驥長鳴，則伯樂照其能；

translations.literal: Your subject has heard that when a thoroughbred neighs long, Bole discerns its power;
translations.idiomatic: They say when a steed trumpets, Bole knows its worth;

sentences.zh: 盧狗悲號，則南韓知其才。

translations.literal: when the Lu mastiff howls in grief, South Han knows its talent.
translations.idiomatic: when the Lu hound bays, the Han hunter marks its skill.

sentences.zh: 是以效之齊、楚之路，以逞千里之任；

translations.literal: Therefore they are tried on the roads of Qi and Chu to display the burden of a thousand li;
translations.idiomatic: So men run them on Qi and Chu roads to prove the thousand-li stride;

sentences.zh: 試之狡兔之捷，以驗搏噬之用。

translations.literal: tested on the cunning hare’s swiftness to verify the use of seizing and biting.
translations.idiomatic: or set them after a swift hare to test their kill.

sentences.zh: 今臣志狗馬之微功，竊自惟度，終無伯樂、南韓之舉，是以於邑而竊自痛者也。

translations.literal: Now your servant aims at dog-and-horse petty merit; privately I reckon that to the end there will be no Bole or South Han to lift me up—therefore I choke with grief and am privately pained.
translations.idiomatic: I ask only the mean service of a dog or horse, yet I see no Bole coming—so I ache in silence.

sentences.zh: 夫臨搏而企竦，聞樂而竊抃者，或有賞音而識道也。

translations.literal: Those who stand on tiptoe at the bout and secretly clap when they hear music—perhaps someone values the tone and knows the Way.
translations.idiomatic: He who cranes at a fight or taps his foot to a tune may still be a true judge of art.

sentences.zh: 昔毛遂，趙之陪隸，猶假錐囊之喻，以寤主立功，何況巍巍大魏多士之朝，而無慷慨死難之臣乎！

translations.literal: Formerly Mao Sui, Zhao’s lowest attendant, still borrowed the awl-in-the-bag parable to awaken his lord and set up merit—how much more in towering Great Wei, a court thick with gentlemen, could there be no minister ardent to die in the state’s hard hour!
translations.idiomatic: Mao Sui was a menial, yet his “awl in the sack” speech won a kingdom—can Wei lack one man ready to die for you?

sentences.zh: 夫自衒自媒者，士女之醜行也。

translations.literal: To hawk oneself and play go-between is an ugly act for gentlemen and ladies alike.
translations.idiomatic: Self-praise and self-sale shame any man or woman.

sentences.zh: 干時求進者，道家之明忌也。

translations.literal: To importune the age seeking promotion is what the Daoists plainly forbid.
translations.idiomatic: To claw for office is what quietist teaching most condemns.

sentences.zh: 而臣敢陳聞於陛下者，誠與國分形同氣，憂患共之者也。

translations.literal: Yet your servant dares lay this before Your Majesty because I truly share one body and one breath with the state and share its sorrows.
translations.idiomatic: I speak because I am bone of your bone—your peril is mine.

sentences.zh: 冀以塵霧之微補益山海，熒燭末光增輝日月，是以敢冒其醜而獻其忠。

translations.literal: I hope with mist-and-dust slightness to add to mountain and sea, with a firefly’s last gleam to lend light to sun and moon—therefore I dare risk shame and offer loyalty.
translations.idiomatic: Let my mite thicken your mountains; let my spark borrow from your sun—this is why I swallow pride and speak.

sentences.zh: 〈《魏略》曰：植雖上此表，猶疑不見用，故曰『夫人貴生者，非貴其養體好服，終竟年壽也，貴在其代天而理物也。

translations.literal: 〈The Weilüe states: Though Zhi presented this memorial, he still doubted it would be employed; therefore he said, “Those who prize life do not prize pampering the body and loving fine dress merely to finish out their years; they prize acting for Heaven to set things in order.
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Weilüe says Zhi feared his words would lie unread, and wrote: “Men who value life value not long years in silks, but doing Heaven’s work in the world.

sentences.zh: 夫爵祿者，非虛張者也，有功德然後應之，當矣。

translations.literal: As for noble rank and salary—they are not empty display; when merit and virtue exist, then one answers them—this is fitting.
translations.idiomatic: Rank and pay are not toys; they follow real merit—that is the rule.

sentences.zh: 無功而爵厚，無德而祿重，或人以為榮，而壯夫以為恥。

translations.literal: Thick rank without merit, heavy salary without virtue—some may deem it glory, stalwarts deem it shame.
translations.idiomatic: Fat office without deeds shames a grown man, though fools may preen.

sentences.zh: 故太上立德，其次立功，蓋功德者所以垂名也。

translations.literal: Therefore highest is establishing virtue, next establishing merit—for merit and virtue are the means to hang down a name.
translations.idiomatic: First plant virtue, then deeds—both are how a name outlives the flesh.

sentences.zh: 名者不滅，士之所利，故孔子有夕死之論，孟軻有棄生之義。

translations.literal: What does not perish is what gentlemen profit by; hence Confucius had the “die at evening” saying, Mencius the meaning of casting away life.
translations.idiomatic: The sage would die at dusk if his name were clear; Mencius would drop life for right.

sentences.zh: 彼一聖一賢，豈不願久生哉？

translations.literal: That one sage and one worthy—did they not wish to live long?
translations.idiomatic: Would Confucius and Mencius have refused long life?

sentences.zh: 志或有不展也。

translations.literal: Sometimes the intent could not unfold.
translations.idiomatic: Their hearts simply had nowhere to go.

sentences.zh: 是用喟然求試，必立功也。

translations.literal: Therefore I sigh and beg trial, resolved to set up merit.
translations.idiomatic: So I beg for a trial—for I mean to earn my keep.

sentences.zh: 嗚呼！

translations.literal: Alas!
translations.idiomatic: Ah—what grief!

sentences.zh: 言之未用，欲使後之君子知吾意者也。〉

translations.literal: My words were not used; I wished gentlemen of later times to know my mind.〉
translations.idiomatic: No one took my counsel; I leave these lines so later men will know my heart.〉

sentences.zh: 三年，徙封東阿。

translations.literal: In the third year he was transferred in enfeoffment to Dong’e.
translations.idiomatic: In 229 he was moved to Dong’e.

sentences.zh: 五年，覆上疏求存問親戚，因致其意曰：

translations.literal: In the fifth year he again submitted a memorial asking permission to inquire after kin, thereby stating his meaning, saying,
translations.idiomatic: In 231 he wrote again, begging leave to visit family and saying:

sentences.zh: 臣聞天稱其高者，以無不覆；

translations.literal: Your subject has heard that Heaven is called high because nothing lies beyond its cover;
translations.idiomatic: Heaven is called high because it roofs all things;

sentences.zh: 地稱其廣者，以無不載；

translations.literal: earth is called vast because nothing lies beyond its bearing;
translations.idiomatic: earth is called wide because it bears all things;

sentences.zh: 日月稱其明者，以無不照；

translations.literal: sun and moon are called bright because nothing lies beyond their shining;
translations.idiomatic: sun and moon are called bright because they light all corners;

sentences.zh: 江海稱其大者，以無不容。

translations.literal: rivers and seas are called great because nothing lies beyond their holding.
translations.idiomatic: the rivers and seas are called great because they hold all streams.

sentences.zh: 故孔子曰：『大哉堯之為君！

translations.literal: Therefore Confucius said, “How great was Yao as lord!
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said: “How great was Yao!

sentences.zh: 惟天為大，惟堯則之。

translations.literal: Only Heaven is great; only Yao modeled himself on it."
translations.idiomatic: Heaven alone is great, and Yao patterned himself on it."

sentences.zh: 』夫天德之於萬物，可謂弘廣矣。

translations.literal: The virtue of Heaven toward the myriad things may be called vast and wide."
translations.idiomatic: Heaven’s kindness to creation is boundless."

sentences.zh: 蓋堯之為教，先親後疏，自近及遠。

translations.literal: In general Yao’s teaching was kin first, distant after, from near reaching far.
translations.idiomatic: Yao taught: cherish kin before strangers, the near before the far.

sentences.zh: 其傳曰：『克明峻德，以親九族；

translations.literal: The transmitted text says, “He brightened his lofty virtue to be intimate with the nine kindreds;"
translations.idiomatic: The canon says: “He spread his bright virtue to draw the nine clans near;"

sentences.zh: 九族既睦，平章百姓。

translations.literal: when the nine kindreds were harmonious, he equalized and illumined the hundred surnames."
translations.idiomatic: when the nine clans were at peace, he brought order to the hundred families."

sentences.zh: 』及周之文王亦崇厥化，其詩曰：『刑於寡妻，至於兄弟，以御於家邦。

translations.literal: And King Wen of Zhou likewise exalted that transformation; his ode says, “He set the model for his wife, extended it to his brothers, thereby to rule house and state."
translations.idiomatic: King Wen did the same; the Odes sing: “He taught wife and brothers, then ruled clan and kingdom."

sentences.zh: 』是以雍雍穆穆。

translations.literal: Therefore there was harmony and solemn dignity."
translations.idiomatic: So harmony filled the hall."

sentences.zh: 風人詠之。

translations.literal: The poets sang of it.
translations.idiomatic: The poets praised it.

sentences.zh: 昔周公弔管、蔡之不咸，廣封懿親以藩屏王室，傳曰：『周之宗盟，異姓為後。

translations.literal: Formerly the Duke of Zhou mourned that Guan and Cai were not harmonious; he broadly enfeoffed dear kin to screen the royal house; the tradition says, “In Zhou’s clan covenants, other surnames came after."
translations.idiomatic: When the Duke of Zhou grieved over Guan and Cai, he packed the realm with kin to fence the throne—the saying runs: “In Zhou’s league, outsiders stood last."

sentences.zh: 』誠骨肉之恩爽而不離，親親之義實在敦固，未有義而後其君，仁而遺其親者也。

translations.literal: Truly the grace of flesh and bone may be distant yet not severed; the duty of loving kin is truly thick and firm—there has never been one who held right yet put his lord last, or held humaneness yet cast off kin."
translations.idiomatic: Kin may wander but the tie holds; no loyal man forgets his prince, no humane man abandons family.

sentences.zh: 伏惟陛下資帝唐欽明之德，體文王翼翼之仁，惠洽椒房，恩昭九族，群後百寮，番休遞上，執政不廢於公朝，下情得展於私室，親理之路通，慶弔之情展，誠可謂恕己治人，推惠施恩者矣。

translations.literal: I humbly reflect that Your Majesty embodies the bright virtue of Emperor Yao, models King Wen’s reverent humaneness, spreads kindness through the pepper chambers, makes grace shine on the nine kindreds; the host of princes and hundred officials rotate rest and attend in turn; governance is not neglected in the public court, private feeling may unfold in inner chambers; paths of kinship are open, joy and mourning may be exchanged—this can truly be called forgiving oneself to govern others and extending favor to spread grace.
translations.idiomatic: You mirror Yao and Wen, bless harem and clan, let princes and ministers take turns at court yet still tend their homes—surely that is the way of mercy.

sentences.zh: 至於臣者，人道絕緒，禁錮明時，臣竊自傷也。

translations.literal: As for your servant, human ties are cut off, I am locked away in this enlightened age; your servant privately wounds for himself.
translations.idiomatic: Yet I alone am severed from kin, caged in this bright reign—I grieve for myself.

sentences.zh: 不敢過望交氣類，脩人事，敘人倫。

translations.literal: I dare not hope beyond matching temperaments, cultivating human affairs, ordering human relations.
translations.idiomatic: I dare not dream of full friendship or ordered ritual among men.

sentences.zh: 近且婚媾不通，兄弟乖絕，吉凶之問塞，慶弔之禮廢，恩紀之違，甚於路人，隔閡之異，殊於胡越。

translations.literal: Lately even marriage ties do not connect, brothers are estranged, inquiries after fortune and woe are blocked, congratulations and condolences cease—the breach of kindly ties is worse than with strangers; the barrier is wider than between Hu and Yue.
translations.idiomatic: We cannot wed across houses, brothers never meet, no word of weal or woe passes—we are colder than strangers, farther apart than north from south.

sentences.zh: 今臣以一切之制，永無朝覲之望，至於註心皇極，結情紫闥，神明知之矣。

translations.literal: Now your servant, under this blanket restriction, forever lacks hope of court audience; as for fixing my heart on the pole star and binding feeling to the purple gate, the spirits know it.
translations.idiomatic: One law bars me from your face forever—yet my heart knots at the palace gate; the gods know it.

sentences.zh: 然天實為之，謂之何哉！

translations.literal: Yet Heaven has made it so—what can be said!
translations.idiomatic: Heaven has willed this—what can I say?

sentences.zh: 退唯諸王常有戚戚具爾之心，願陛下沛然垂詔，使諸國慶問，四節得展，以敘骨肉之歡恩。

translations.literal: Stepping back, I trust the various kings always harbor the “we two” anxious heart; I hope Your Majesty will abundantly issue an edict so the states may exchange congratulations, the four seasons find expression, and thereby order the joy and grace of flesh and bone.
translations.idiomatic: I know my royal brothers ache as I do; send one generous edict so princes may visit at the seasons and feel human warmth again.

sentences.zh: 全怡怡之篤義。

translations.literal: Complete the earnest meaning of cordial joy.
translations.idiomatic: Restore the easy love of kinsmen.

sentences.zh: 妃妾之家，膏沐之遺，歲得再通，齊義於貴宗，等惠於百司，如此，則古人之所嘆，風雅之所詠，復存於聖世矣。

translations.literal: In consorts’ households, the gift of scented unguents, twice a year may communicate; align duty with the honored clan, match kindness with the hundred offices—if so, then what men of old sighed over, what the Feng and Ya chant, will again exist in this sagely age.
translations.idiomatic: Let wives’ kin exchange gifts twice a year, treat them like great houses, share bounty with officials—then the Odes’ praise of family love will live again in our day.

sentences.zh: 臣伏自惟省，無錐刀之用。

translations.literal: Your servant humbly reflects on himself and finds no use even of an awl’s point.
translations.idiomatic: I know I am not worth a knife-tip’s service.

sentences.zh: 及觀陛下之所拔授，若以臣為異姓，竊自料度，不後於朝士矣。

translations.literal: Yet observing those Your Majesty promotes, if I were reckoned another surname, I would privately measure myself as not behind court gentlemen.
translations.idiomatic: Yet those you raise from outside the blood—I do not think myself less than they.

sentences.zh: 若得辭遠游，戴武弁，解朱組，佩青紱，駙馬、奉車，趣得一號，安宅京室，執鞭珥筆，出從華蓋，入侍輦轂，承答聖問，拾遺左右，乃臣丹誠之至願，不離於夢想者也。

translations.literal: If I could leave distant roaming, don the martial cap, undo the vermillion cord, wear the green cord, serve as side-car horse or carriage attendant, hasten to obtain one title, dwell in peace in the capital, hold whip and tuck brush, go out following the flowered canopy, enter and attend the imperial axle-hubs, answer sagely questions, pick up omissions at left and right—this is your servant’s utmost crimson loyalty’s desire, never leaving his dreams.
translations.idiomatic: Let me shed my princedom, wear a soldier’s cap or clerk’s green, tend your chariot, keep house in Luoyang, take notes at your stirrup—this is the prayer I mutter in sleep.

sentences.zh: 遠慕鹿鳴君臣之宴，中詠常棣匪他之誡，下思伐木友生之義，終懷蓼莪罔極之哀；

translations.literal: From afar I admire the lord-and-minister feast in “Deer Call,” in the middle chant the “Not other” warning in “Changdi,” below ponder the “Friend born” sense in “Felling Trees,” and to the end cherish the “boundless” grief in “Thick Motherwort;"
translations.idiomatic: High I long for the “Deer Call” feast; mid I heed “Changdi’s” warning; low I recall “Felling Trees” friendship; always I mourn like “Thick Motherwort’s” child;

sentences.zh: 每四節之會，塊然獨處，左右惟僕隸，所對惟妻子，高談無所與陳，發義無所與展，未嘗不聞樂而拊心，臨觴而嘆息也。

translations.literal: at each meeting of the four seasons, alone and lumpish I sit; at my sides only slaves; those I face only wife and children; I have no one with whom to set forth lofty talk, no one with whom to unfold right principles—never do I fail to strike my breast at hearing music, sigh over the cup when wine comes.
translations.idiomatic: each quarter-day I sit alone with servants and wives, no friend for high talk—so music wrings my heart and wine draws only sighs.

sentences.zh: 臣伏以為犬馬之誠不能動人，譬人之誠不能動天。

translations.literal: Your servant humbly thinks that dog-and-horse sincerity cannot move others, just as worm sincerity cannot move Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: A dog’s loyalty does not sway men; a gnat’s zeal does not move Heaven.

sentences.zh: 崩城、隕霜，臣初信之，以臣心況，徒虛語耳。

translations.literal: Walls collapsing and frost falling—your servant at first believed them; measured against my heart, they are mere empty talk.
translations.idiomatic: I once believed tales of cities crumbling to grief and frost from wronged wives—against my own case, they ring hollow.

sentences.zh: 若葵藿之傾葉，太陽雖不為之回光，然向之者誠也。

translations.literal: As hollyhock and bean lean their leaves—though the great sun does not turn its light for them, yet those that face it are sincere.
translations.idiomatic: Sunflowers turn to the sun though the sun does not turn to them—still they are true.

sentences.zh: 竊自比於葵藿，若降天地之施，垂三光之明者，實在陛下。

translations.literal: Your servant privately compares himself to hollyhock and bean; if there is one who lets fall Heaven and Earth’s bounty and sheds the three luminaries’ brightness, it is truly Your Majesty.
translations.idiomatic: I am that sunflower; if any grace falls, it falls from you alone.

sentences.zh: 臣聞文子曰：『不為福始，不為禍先。

translations.literal: Your subject has heard Master Wenzi say, “Do not be the first to seek fortune, nor the first to invite disaster."
translations.idiomatic: Wenzi said: “Do not court fortune, do not court ruin."

sentences.zh: 』今之否隔，友於同憂，而臣獨倡言者，竊不願於聖世使有不蒙施之物。

translations.literal: Now this blockage—brothers share one grief—yet your servant alone speaks first because I privately would not have, in this sagely age, a thing that receives no bounty.
translations.idiomatic: Brothers all suffer this wall—yet I speak first, for I cannot bear that any soul miss your rain in a reign like yours.

sentences.zh: 有不蒙施之物，必有慘毒之懷，故柏舟有『天只』之怨，穀風有『棄予』之嘆。

translations.literal: Where there is a thing that receives no bounty, there must be hearts of bitter poison; therefore the “Cypress Boat” has the “Heaven above” resentment, “Valley Wind” the “you cast me” sigh.
translations.idiomatic: Neglect breeds poison—the Odes knew it in “Cypress Boat” and “Valley Wind.”

sentences.zh: 故伊尹恥其君不為堯舜，孟子曰：『不以舜之所以事堯事其君者，不敬其君者也。

translations.literal: Therefore Yi Yin was ashamed his lord was not Yao or Shun; Mencius said, “He who does not serve his lord with the way Shun served Yao does not respect his lord."
translations.idiomatic: Yi Yin blushed for any king less than Yao; Mencius said serving a prince without Shun’s zeal is disrespect.

sentences.zh: 』臣之愚蔽，固非虞、伊，至於欲使陛下崇光被時雍之美，宣緝熙章明之德者，是臣慺慺之誠，竊所獨守，實懷鶴立企佇之心。

translations.literal: Your servant’s foolish blindness is surely not that of Yu or Yi; as for wishing to make Your Majesty exalt the beauty of spreading light and bringing timely harmony, and proclaim the bright virtue of gathering splendor—this is your servant’s earnest sincerity, what he alone guards, and in truth he harbors a heart of crane-standing, heel-lifted waiting.
translations.idiomatic: I am no sage, yet I beg you to shine like Yao and spread harmony—I stand like a crane on one leg, waiting.

sentences.zh: 敢復陳聞者，冀陛下儻發天聰而垂神聽也。

translations.literal: I dare lay this again before you, hoping Your Majesty may perhaps open Heaven’s hearing and bend divine ear.
translations.idiomatic: I speak again, praying you will listen once.

sentences.zh: 詔報曰：『蓋教化所由，各有隆弊，非皆善始而惡終也，事使之然。

translations.literal: An edict replied, saying, “As for what transformation follows, each has its height and decline—not all begin well and end ill; affairs make it so.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor answered: “Ways of rule rise and fall—not every age turns sour; circumstance shapes them.

sentences.zh: 故夫忠厚仁極草木，則行葦之詩作；

translations.literal: Therefore when loyalty and kindness reach utmost even plants and trees, then the ode ‘Walking Rushes’ was made;
translations.idiomatic: When kindness ran deep even to reeds, poets sang “Walking Rushes”;

sentences.zh: 恩澤衰薄，不親九族，則角弓之章刺。

translations.literal: when favor ran thin and the nine kindreds were not cherished, then the stanza ‘Horn Bow’ satirized.
translations.idiomatic: when kin grew cold, they satirized it in “Horn Bow.”

sentences.zh: 今令諸國兄弟，情理簡怠，妃妾之家，膏沐疏略，朕縱不能敦而睦之，王援古喻義備悉矣，何言精誠不足以感通哉？

translations.literal: Now I order the fraternal princes: feeling and duty have grown slack; consorts’ households lack frequent gifts of scented unguents; though I cannot myself enrich and harmonize them, you, my king, citing antiquity and paralleling meaning have set it all forth—how can you say true sincerity cannot penetrate?"
translations.idiomatic: I have let brotherly love grow thin and neglected gifts between in-laws—you have argued from the Odes with full right; can you say the heart cannot reach?"

sentences.zh: 夫明貴賤，崇親親，禮賢良，順少長，國之綱紀，本無禁固諸國通問之詔也，矯枉過正，下吏懼譴，以至於此耳。

translations.literal: To clarify noble and base, honor kin, treat worthies well, and order young and old—these are the state’s guiding cords; originally there was no edict forbidding the princes mutual inquiry, but in straightening the crooked we overshot, lower clerks feared blame, and it came to this."
translations.idiomatic: Clarifying rank, cherishing kin, honoring talent, and ordering age are the law’s spine—no edict ever meant to seal your doors; over-correction and timid clerks did that."

sentences.zh: 已敕有司，如王所訴。

translations.literal: I have already ordered the responsible offices according to what the king pleaded."
translations.idiomatic: I have told the ministries to grant what you ask."

sentences.zh: 』植覆上疏陳審舉之義，曰：臣聞天地協氣而萬物生，君臣合德而庶政成；

translations.literal: Zhi again submitted a memorial setting forth the meaning of careful selection, saying: Your subject hears that when Heaven and Earth blend their breath the myriad things are born, when lord and minister unite in virtue the multitude of tasks is completed;
translations.idiomatic: Zhi wrote again on choosing officials: “Heaven and earth’s breath makes the world live; ruler and minister in tune make government work;

sentences.zh: 五帝之世非皆智，三季之末非皆愚，用與不用，知與不知也。

translations.literal: in the age of the Five Thearchs not all were wise, in the last days of the three dynasties not all were stupid—use and non-use, knowing and not knowing.
translations.idiomatic: the Five Thearchs’ court was not all sages, the last kings’ not all fools—it is use and insight that matter.

sentences.zh: 既時有舉賢之名，而無得賢之實，必各援其類而進矣。

translations.literal: Since the times bear the name of raising worthies yet lack the reality of obtaining worthies, each will surely advance his own kind.
translations.idiomatic: When “raising worthies” is only a slogan, every man promotes his own pack.

sentences.zh: 諺曰：『相門有相，將門有將。

translations.literal: The proverb says, “A minister’s house breeds ministers, a general’s house breeds generals."
translations.idiomatic: The proverb runs: “Prime ministers beget prime ministers, generals beget generals."

sentences.zh: 』夫相者，文德昭者也；

translations.literal: A minister is one whose patterned virtue shines;
translations.idiomatic: A minister shines in civil virtue;

sentences.zh: 將者，武功烈者也。

translations.literal: a general is one whose martial merit blazes.
translations.idiomatic: a general blazes in martial deeds.

sentences.zh: 文德昭，則可以匡國朝，致雍熙，稷、契、夔、龍是也；

translations.literal: When patterned virtue shines, then he can rectify the court and bring harmonious splendor—Ji, Qi, Kui, and Long were such;
translations.idiomatic: Civil men set the court straight—think of Ji and Qi;

sentences.zh: 武功烈，則所以征不庭，威四夷，南仲、方叔是矣。

translations.literal: when martial merit blazes, then he can punish those who do not attend court and awe the four barbarians—Nanzhong and Fangshu were such.
translations.idiomatic: martial men chastise rebels—think of Nanzhong and Fangshu.

sentences.zh: 昔伊尹之為媵臣，至賤也，呂尚之處屠釣，至陋也，及其見舉於湯武、周文，誠道合志同，玄謨神通，豈復假近習之薦，因左右之介哉。

translations.literal: Formerly Yi Yin served as a concubine’s cook—utterly base; Lü Shang stood among butchers and anglers—utterly low; yet when they were raised by Tang and Wu and King Wen, it was truly that the Way matched and aims joined, dark plans touched spirits—how could they have relied on nearness of habit or introduction by attendants?
translations.idiomatic: Yi Yin was a cook, Lü Wang a peddler—yet Tang and Wen raised them; heart met heart, no need of petty introductions.

sentences.zh: 書曰：『有不世之君，必能用不世之臣；

translations.literal: The document says, “When there is a lord not of a common generation, he can employ ministers not of a common generation;"
translations.idiomatic: The classic says: “A matchless king uses matchless servants;

sentences.zh: 用不世之臣，必能立不世之功。

translations.literal: when he employs ministers not of a common generation, he can set up merit not of a common generation."
translations.idiomatic: matchless servants win matchless deeds."

sentences.zh: 』殷周二王是矣。

translations.literal: The two kings of Yin and Zhou were such."
translations.idiomatic: So it was for Yin and Zhou."

sentences.zh: 若夫齷齪近步，遵常守故，安足為陛下言哉？

translations.literal: As for petty cramped short steps, following the constant and guarding the old—how can that suffice to speak to Your Majesty?"
translations.idiomatic: Small men hug routine—why waste your ear on them?"

sentences.zh: 故陰陽不和，三光不暢，官曠無人，庶政不整者，三司之責也。

translations.literal: When yin and yang are not in harmony, the three luminaries do not shine clear, offices stand empty and none fill them, the multitude of tasks lack order—these are the Three Excellencies’ burden.
translations.idiomatic: When yin and yang clash, stars dim, posts stand empty, and policy drifts—the Three Dukes have failed.

sentences.zh: 疆埸騷動，方隅內侵，沒軍喪眾，干戈不息者，邊將之憂也。

translations.literal: When the borderlands seethe, corners within are invaded, armies perish and hosts are lost, spears and shields do not rest—these are border generals’ worries.
translations.idiomatic: When frontiers boil, invaders cross, armies die, and war never ends—the field commanders have failed.

sentences.zh: 豈可虛荷國寵而不稱其任哉？

translations.literal: How can one vainly bear the state’s favor yet not answer the charge?
translations.idiomatic: How bear the state’s pay and not pay the debt?

sentences.zh: 故任益隆者負益重，位益高者責益深，書稱『無曠庶官』，詩有『職思其憂』，此其義也。

translations.literal: Therefore the higher the charge the heavier the burden, the higher the station the deeper the responsibility—the document speaks of “no idle multitude of offices,” the Odes have “in office think its sorrows”—this is the meaning.
translations.idiomatic: Higher rank means heavier blame—the Documents warn against empty chairs, the Odes tell officers to dread their charge.

sentences.zh: 陛下體天真之淑聖，登神機以繼統，冀聞康哉之歌，偃武行文之美。

translations.literal: Your Majesty embodies Heaven’s truth, pure sagely perfection, mounts the divine pivot to continue the line, and hopes to hear the song of “How vast,” to lay down arms and unfold pattern’s beauty.
translations.idiomatic: You are sage and true heir—you mean to hear “How vast,” to trade spears for laws.

sentences.zh: 而數年以來，水旱不時，民困衣食，師徒之發，歲歲增調，加東有覆敗之軍，西有殪沒之將，至使蚌蛤浮翔於淮、泗，鼲鼬讙嘩於林木。

translations.literal: Yet for several years flood and drought have not kept season, the people are hard pressed in clothing and food, army expeditions are levied year on year increasing, and moreover to the east there was an army overturned in defeat, to the west generals who perished to the last man—so that clams float on Huai and Si, weasels squeal in the woods.
translations.idiomatic: Yet flood and famine follow, the people hunger, levies mount, eastern hosts are routed, western generals die—and omens rise: shellfish on the Si, vermin in the wood.

sentences.zh: 臣每念之，未嘗不輟食而揮餐，臨觴而搤腕矣。

translations.literal: Whenever your subject thinks on it, never do I fail to stop eating and push away my meal, face the cup and clutch my wrist.
translations.idiomatic: Each time I think of it I push my food away and grip my wrist over the wine.

sentences.zh: 昔漢文發代，疑朝有變，宋昌曰：『內有朱虛、東牟之親，外有齊、楚、淮南、琅邪，此則磐石之宗，願王勿疑。

translations.literal: Formerly when Emperor Wen of Han set out from Dai, he suspected change in court; Song Chang said, “Within you have the kin of Zhu Xu and Dongmou; without you have Qi, Chu, Huainan, and Langye—these are the clan’s bedrock stones; I pray the king have no doubt."
translations.idiomatic: When Han Wendi came from Dai, Song Chang told him: “Inside you have stalwart kin; outside lie great fiefs—you are rock; do not fear."

sentences.zh: 』臣伏惟陛下遠覽姬文二虢之援，中慮周成召、畢之輔，下存宋昌磐石之固。

translations.literal: Your subject humbly hopes Your Majesty will look far to King Wen of Zhou’s aid from the two Guo, weigh midmost King Cheng’s helpers the Dukes of Shao and Bi, and keep below Song Chang’s bedrock solidity.
translations.idiomatic: Look high to Wen’s use of Guo, think mid to Cheng’s use of Shao and Bi, remember low how Song Chang steadied the Han throne.

sentences.zh: 昔騏驥之於吳阪，可謂困矣，及其伯樂相之，孫郵御之，形體不勞而坐取千里。

translations.literal: Formerly the thoroughbred on Wu’s slope could be called trapped, yet when Bole judged him and Sun You drove him, his frame knew no toil yet he sat and took a thousand li.
translations.idiomatic: A steed on Wu Slope was spent—yet Bole picked him, Sun You drove him, and he flew a thousand li untired.

sentences.zh: 蓋伯樂善御馬，明君善御臣；

translations.literal: In general Bole was good at governing horses, the enlightened lord good at governing ministers;
translations.idiomatic: Bole mastered horses; the wise king masters men;

sentences.zh: 伯樂馳千里，明君致太平；

translations.literal: Bole made a thousand li gallop; the enlightened lord brings Great Peace;
translations.idiomatic: Bole drew out a thousand li; the king draws out the Great Peace;

sentences.zh: 誠任賢使能之明效也。

translations.literal: truly it is the clear effect of appointing worthies and employing the able.
translations.idiomatic: proof that right men in right posts make the realm whole."

sentences.zh: 若朝司惟良，萬機內理，武將行師，方難克弭。

translations.literal: If court ministers are all excellent, the myriad threads are ordered within, martial generals take the field, then frontier hardships can be quelled.
translations.idiomatic: Fit ministers, smooth government, able generals—and border troubles melt away.

sentences.zh: 陛下可得雍容都城，何事勞動鑾駕，暴露於邊境哉？

translations.literal: Your Majesty could then dwell at ease in the capital—why should you trouble the imperial equipage and expose yourself on the borders?
translations.idiomatic: You could keep your majesty in Luoyang; why ride the war train to the marches?

sentences.zh: 臣聞羊質虎皮，見草則悅，見豺則戰，忘其皮之虎也。

translations.literal: Your subject has heard: a sheep in tiger skin delights at grass yet quails at jackals, forgetting its coat is tiger.
translations.idiomatic: A sheep dressed as a tiger still loves grass and fears wolves—it forgets the disguise.

sentences.zh: 今置將不良，有似於此。

translations.literal: Now in appointing generals badly, the case is much the same.
translations.idiomatic: Bad appointments of commanders are the same folly.

sentences.zh: 故語曰：『患為之者不知，知之者不得為也。

translations.literal: Hence the saying: "The one who suffers the harm does not understand; the one who understands cannot act."
translations.idiomatic: The proverb runs: fools suffer what sages see—but cannot fix.

sentences.zh: 』昔樂毅奔趙，心不忘燕；

translations.literal: Formerly Yue Yi fled to Zhao yet his heart did not forget Yan;
translations.idiomatic: Yue Yi fled to Zhao but his heart stayed in Yan;

sentences.zh: 廉頗在楚，思為趙將。

translations.literal: Lian Po was in Chu yet longed to be Zhao’s general.
translations.idiomatic: Lian Po, an exile in Chu, begged to lead Zhao’s spears again.

sentences.zh: 臣生乎亂，長乎軍，又數承教於武皇帝，伏見行師用兵之要，不必取孫、吳而闇與之合。

translations.literal: Your servant was born in chaos, reared in armies, and often received Emperor Wu’s teaching; I humbly observed the essentials of campaign and combat—one need not quote Sun and Wu yet may silently match them.
translations.idiomatic: I grew up under arms with Emperor Wu’s lessons—I know war’s heart without reciting Sunzi.

sentences.zh: 竊揆之於心，常願得一奉朝覲，排金門，蹈玉陛，列有職之臣，賜須臾之問，使臣得一散所懷，攄舒蘊積，死不恨矣。

translations.literal: Privately I gauge my heart: I ever hope once to attend court, pass the Golden Gate, tread the jade steps, stand among titled officials, win a moment’s audience, pour out what I hoard, vent what is pent—then death would hold no regret.
translations.idiomatic: I ask only one audience—to cross your threshold, speak my piece, and die content.

sentences.zh: 被鴻臚所下發士息書，期會甚急。

translations.literal: I received the Grand Herald’s order dispatching soldier-sons; the deadline was very tight.
translations.idiomatic: The Herald’s levy order came with a cruel deadline.

sentences.zh: 又聞豹尾已建，戎軒騖駕，陛下將復勞玉躬，擾掛神思。

translations.literal: I also hear the leopard-tail host is raised and the war chariot races—Your Majesty will again weary your sacred person and rack your mind.
translations.idiomatic: Word says your banner marches and you mean to take the field again—my heart fails me.

sentences.zh: 臣誠竦息，不遑寧處。

translations.literal: Your servant truly stands breathless with fear and cannot find rest.
translations.idiomatic: I tremble and cannot sit still.

sentences.zh: 願得策馬執鞭，首當塵露，撮風後之奇，接孫、吳之要，追慕卜商起予左右，效命先驅，畢命輪轂，雖無大益，冀有小補。

translations.literal: I wish to whip a horse and grip the lash, meet the first dust and dew, seize Feng Hou’s marvels, link Sun and Wu’s essentials, emulate Bu Shang who roused Confucius at his side, give life as vanguard, spend life at the wheel-hub—though without great gain, I hope for small help.
translations.idiomatic: Let me ride first, take your dust, use what I learned from Wu—die at the van if you will; even a little use would suffice.

sentences.zh: 然天高聽遠，情不上通，徒獨望青雲而拊心，仰高天而嘆息耳。

translations.literal: Yet Heaven is high and hearing distant; feeling does not rise to meet you—I only gaze at the clouds, strike my breast, and sigh toward the sky.
translations.idiomatic: Yet you are far as heaven; my words never rise—I beat my breast at empty sky.

sentences.zh: 屈平曰：『國有驥而不知乘，焉皇皇而更索！

translations.literal: Qu Yuan said: "The state owns a steed yet will not ride it—why scour the road for another?"
translations.idiomatic: Qu Yuan cried: "You keep a thoroughbred in the stable yet hunt for nags!"

sentences.zh: 』昔管、蔡放誅，周、召作弼；

translations.literal: Formerly Guan and Cai were cast out and killed, yet the Dukes of Zhou and Shao became bulwarks;
translations.idiomatic: When Guan and Cai fell, Zhou and Shao still held the house;

sentences.zh: 叔魚陷刑，叔向匡國。

translations.literal: Shuyu fell under sentence, yet Shuxiang saved the state.
translations.idiomatic: Shuyu went to the block; Shuxiang righted Jin.

sentences.zh: 三監之釁，臣自當之；

translations.literal: The Three Overseers’ guilt—your servant will bear it himself;
translations.idiomatic: If the Three Overseers’ guilt returns, let it fall on me;

sentences.zh: 二南之輔，求必不遠。

translations.literal: aides like those of the Two Souths—seek them and they are not far.
translations.idiomatic: helpers like the Odes’ southern masters—surely they stand near at hand.

sentences.zh: 華宗貴族，藩王之中，必有應斯舉者。

translations.literal: Among great clans and enfeoffed kings there must be men fit for this charge.
translations.idiomatic: Among your kinsmen-princes someone can answer this call.

sentences.zh: 故傳曰：『無周公之親，不得行周公之事。

translations.literal: The tradition says: "Without the Duke of Zhou’s kinship, one may not do the Duke of Zhou’s work."
translations.idiomatic: The old text says: no Zhou kin, no Zhou-sized task.

sentences.zh: 』唯陛下少留意焉。

translations.literal: Only may Your Majesty bend a little thought to it."
translations.idiomatic: I beg you weigh these words."

sentences.zh: 近者漢氏廣建藩王，豐則連城數十，約則饗食祖祭而已，未若姬周之樹國，五等之品制之。

translations.literal: In late times Han broadly enfeoffed princes—rich ones held dozens of linked cities, poor ones barely kept ancestral sacrifice; it never matched Zhou’s graded tree of states and five ranks.
translations.idiomatic: Han’s princes ran from vast domains to mere temple stipends—nothing like Zhou’s ordered ladder of lords.

sentences.zh: 若扶蘇之諫始皇，淳于越之難周青臣，可謂知時變矣。

translations.literal: Like Fusu’s warning to the First Emperor or Chunyu Yue’s rebuke of Zhou Qingchen—they knew the times were changing.
translations.idiomatic: Fusu and Chunyu Yue read the turning tide—so should we.

sentences.zh: 夫能使天下傾耳註目者，當權者是矣，故謀能移主，威能懾下。

translations.literal: He who makes the realm cock ear and fix eye is he who holds power; therefore counsel can sway the throne, terror can cow the ranks.
translations.idiomatic: Power draws every eye; plots move kings, dread rules ministers.

sentences.zh: 豪右執政，不在親戚；

translations.literal: When magnates rule, it is not kin who hold the levers;
translations.idiomatic: Great houses seize the wheel—not your blood kin;

sentences.zh: 權之所在，雖疏必重，勢之所去，雖親必輕，蓋取齊者田族，非呂宗也。

translations.literal: where power sits, though distant they weigh heavy; where it leaves, though close they grow light—for Tian took Qi, not the house of Lü.
translations.idiomatic: Power makes strangers heavy and kin light—the Tian stole Qi, not the Lü.

sentences.zh: 分晉者趙、魏，非姬姓也。

translations.literal: Those who carved up Jin were Zhao and Wei, not the Ji surname.
translations.idiomatic: Jin fell to Zhao and Wei, not to Zhou’s own line.

sentences.zh: 唯陛下察之。

translations.literal: Only may Your Majesty examine this.
translations.idiomatic: Consider this, I pray.

sentences.zh: 苟吉專其位，凶離其患者，異姓之臣也。

translations.literal: Those who cling to office in good fortune yet flee the ruler’s peril in evil fortune are ministers of other surnames.
translations.idiomatic: Outsiders ride your luck and quit your storm.

sentences.zh: 欲國之安，祈家之貴，存共其榮，沒同其禍者，公族之臣也。

translations.literal: Those who pray for the state’s peace, seek the clan’s honor, share glory alive and share ruin dead are ministers of the royal house.
translations.idiomatic: Kin sink or swim with the throne—that is our kind.

sentences.zh: 今反公族疏而異姓親，臣竊惑焉。

translations.literal: Now kin are kept cold while outsiders are warmed—your servant is privately bewildered.
translations.idiomatic: Today you favor strangers and chill your brothers—I cannot understand it.

sentences.zh: 臣聞孟子曰：『君子窮則獨善其身，達則兼善天下。

translations.literal: Your subject has heard Mencius say: "The gentleman in straits perfects himself alone; in success he shares good with the world."
translations.idiomatic: Mencius said: the noble man mends himself in poverty and blesses the world when risen.

sentences.zh: 』今臣與陛下踐冰履炭，登山浮澗，寒溫燥濕，高下共之，豈得離陛下哉？

translations.literal: Now your servant and Your Majesty tread ice and walk coals, climb hills and ford streams, cold, heat, wet, dry, high, low—we share them—how could I leave Your Majesty?
translations.idiomatic: You and I have shared ice and fire, hill and flood—how should I part from you now?

sentences.zh: 不勝憤懣，拜表陳情。

translations.literal: Unable to bear my pent wrath, I bow and lay this feeling before you.
translations.idiomatic: I choke on rage and set it down in this memorial.

sentences.zh: 若有不合，乞且藏之書府，不便滅棄，臣死之後，事或可思。

translations.literal: If it misses the mark, I beg you file it in the archive, not cast it away; after I die, perhaps men will ponder it.
translations.idiomatic: If it offends, shelve it, do not burn it—after my death it may be read.

sentences.zh: 若有豪釐少掛聖意者，乞出之朝堂，使夫博古之士，糾臣表之不合義者。

translations.literal: If a hair’s breadth touches your mind, bring it to open court and let scholars versed in antiquity pick apart where my words fail justice.
translations.idiomatic: If a line rings false, publish it and let the learned correct me in daylight.

sentences.zh: 如是，則臣願足矣。

translations.literal: If so, your servant’s wish is complete.
translations.idiomatic: That would fulfill my prayer.

sentences.zh: 帝輒優文答報。

translations.literal: The Emperor always answered with gracious edicts.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor always replied with kind words.

sentences.zh: 〈《魏略》曰：是後大發士息，及取諸國士。

translations.literal: 〈The Weilüe states: After this a great levy of soldier-sons was issued, and men were taken from the princes’ domains.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈The Weilüe: then came the great draft of princes’ household troops.〉

sentences.zh: 植以近前諸國士息已見發，孤稚弱，在者無幾，而復被取，乃上書曰：『臣聞古者聖君，與日月齊其明，四時等其信，是以戮凶無重，賞善無輕，怒若驚霆，喜若時雨，恩不中絕，教無二可，以此臨朝，則臣下知所死矣。

translations.literal: Zhi, because recently the various states’ soldier-sons had already been levied, leaving orphans few and weak, with hardly any left, and yet were taken again, therefore submitted a memorial, saying: "Your subject has heard that in antiquity the sage lord shared brightness with sun and moon and faith with the four seasons; therefore punishing the wicked was never too heavy, rewarding the good never too light; anger like startling thunder, joy like seasonable rain—grace never cut off midstream, teaching never double-tongued; with this facing court, ministers knew where to die."
translations.idiomatic: Zhi wrote again: the ancient sage matched sun and moon in justice and the seasons in promise—punishment sure, reward swift—so every servant knew where to lay down his life.

sentences.zh: 受任在萬里之外，審主之所授官，必己之所以投命，雖有構會之徒，泊然不以為懼者，蓋君臣相信之明效也。

translations.literal: Receiving charge beyond ten thousand li, examining the offices the lord confers, surely matching what one pledges life to—even if slanderers gather, one remains calm and unafraid—this is the clear effect of lord and minister trusting each other.
translations.idiomatic: A man sent far trusts his orders; even slander cannot shake him—that is true faith between prince and servant.

sentences.zh: 昔章子為齊將，人有告之反者，威王曰：「不然。

translations.literal: Formerly Tian Zhang served as Qi’s general; someone reported him rebellious; King Wei said, "It is not so."
translations.idiomatic: When someone slandered Tian Zhang to King Wei of Qi, the king said no.

sentences.zh: 」左右曰：「王何以明之？

translations.literal: Those at his side said, "How does the king know?"
translations.idiomatic: His attendants asked how he knew.

sentences.zh: 」王曰：「聞章子改葬死母；

translations.literal: The king said, "I hear Tian Zhang reburied his dead mother with a change of rites;"
translations.idiomatic: He said: “Zhang would not cheat his dead mother’s grave—

sentences.zh: 彼尚不欺死父，顧當叛生君乎？

translations.literal: he would not deceive a dead father—would he turn on a living lord?"
translations.idiomatic: would he betray a living king?”

sentences.zh: 」此君之信臣也。

translations.literal: This is the lord’s faith in his minister."
translations.idiomatic: That is a lord who trusts his man."

sentences.zh: 昔管仲親射桓公，後幽囚從魯檻車載，使少年輓而送齊。

translations.literal: Formerly Guan Zhong himself shot Duke Huan, later was imprisoned and carried from Lu in a caged cart, youths hauling him to Qi.
translations.idiomatic: Guan Zhong once shot Huan, then rode to Qi in Lu’s cage-cart, boys hauling the rope.

sentences.zh: 管仲知桓公之必用己，懼魯之悔，謂少年曰：「吾為汝唱，汝為和，聲和聲，宜走。

translations.literal: Guan Zhong knew Duke Huan would surely use him, feared Lu would repent, and told the youths, "I will lead the song, you harmonize; when voice matches voice, you should run."
translations.idiomatic: Knowing Huan would use him and Lu might change its mind, he told the boys to run in time to his chant.

sentences.zh: 」於是管仲唱之，少年走而和之，日行數百裡，宿昔而至。

translations.literal: Thereupon Guan Zhong sang and the youths ran harmonizing; in a day they covered several hundred li, and by the next night they arrived.
translations.idiomatic: They ran hundreds of li a day to his song and reached Qi overnight.

sentences.zh: 至則相齊，此臣之信君也。

translations.literal: Arrived, he became Qi’s minister—this is the minister’s faith in his lord."
translations.idiomatic: He became Huan’s minister—faith cuts both ways."

sentences.zh: 臣初受封，策書曰：「植受茲青社，封於東土，以屏翰皇家，為魏藩輔。

translations.literal: When your servant first received enfeoffment, the investiture document said, "Zhi receives this green altar-soil, is enfeoffed in the eastern lands, to screen and brace the imperial house, to be Wei’s bulwark."
translations.idiomatic: My patent read: “You take the green soil of the east to fence the royal house.”

sentences.zh: 」而所得兵百五十人，皆年在耳順，或不逾矩，虎賁官騎及親事凡二百餘人。

translations.literal: Yet the soldiers obtained numbered only one hundred fifty, all past their sixtieth year or near it, plus tiger-guard riders and personal attendants in all a bit over two hundred.
translations.idiomatic: Yet I was given one hundred fifty troops, all past sixty, plus two hundred guards—every man gray.

sentences.zh: 正復不老，皆使年壯，備有不虞，檢校乘城，顧不足以自救，況皆復耄耋罷曳乎？

translations.literal: Even were they not old, were all made in their prime, prepared against the unforeseen, to inspect and man the walls—still it would not suffice to save themselves; how much more when all are doddering and feeble?
translations.idiomatic: Even young men could not hold my walls; these ancients could not save themselves, let alone you.

sentences.zh: 而名為魏東藩，使屏翰王室，臣竊自羞矣。

translations.literal: Yet my name is Wei’s eastern bulwark, charged to screen the royal house—your servant is privately ashamed.
translations.idiomatic: You call me the eastern shield—yet I blush at the jest.

sentences.zh: 就之諸國，國有士子，合不過五百人。

translations.literal: Taken together among the states, each state’s gentlemen-soldiers do not exceed five hundred.
translations.idiomatic: All princes together can muster fewer than five hundred fit men.

sentences.zh: 伏以為三軍益損，不復賴此。

translations.literal: I humbly think the three armies’ increase or decrease no longer depends on this.
translations.idiomatic: The hosts do not need these few souls.

sentences.zh: 方外不定，必當須辦者，臣願將部曲倍道奔赴，夫妻負襁，子弟懷糧，蹈鋒履刃，以徇國難，何但習業小兒哉？

translations.literal: When matters beyond the frontiers are unsettled and men must be mustered, your servant wishes to lead his retainers at double march to rush there, wives carrying infants, sons bearing grain, treading blades and walking edges to follow the state through disaster—how could they be only boys in training?
translations.idiomatic: If war calls, I will march my whole household at double time—wives, babes, grain sacks—not “schoolboys.”

sentences.zh: 愚誠以揮涕增河，鼷鼠飲海，於朝萬無損益，於臣家計甚有廢損。

translations.literal: My foolish sincerity is like weeping to swell a river, a shrew-mouse drinking the sea—toward court it adds or subtracts nothing; toward my household’s economy it greatly wastes and harms.
translations.idiomatic: My tears cannot fill a river; my mice cannot drain the sea—this levy helps you not at all and ruins me.

sentences.zh: 又臣士息前後三送，兼人已竭。

translations.literal: Moreover your servant’s soldier-sons have been sent off three times in succession; the able-bodied are already exhausted.
translations.idiomatic: You have taken my men three times; the strong are gone.

sentences.zh: 惟尚有小兒，七八歲已上，十六七已還，三十餘人。

translations.literal: Only there remain small boys, above seven or eight sui, up to sixteen or seventeen, a bit over thirty.
translations.idiomatic: Only thirty-odd boys from eight to sixteen remain.

sentences.zh: 今部曲皆年耆，卧在床席，非糜不食，眼不能視，氣息裁屬者，凡三十七人；

translations.literal: Now the retainers are all aged, lying on beds, eating only gruel, eyes unable to see, breath barely continuous—thirty-seven such;
translations.idiomatic: Thirty-seven are bedridden, half blind, barely breathing;

sentences.zh: 疲瘵風靡，疣盲聾聵者，二十三人。

translations.literal: worn sick, wind-paralyzed, warty, blind, deaf—twenty-three such.
translations.idiomatic: twenty-three are crippled, deaf, or blind.

sentences.zh: 惟正須此小兒，大者可備宿衛，雖不足以禦寇，粗可以警小盜；

translations.literal: Only these small boys are truly needed; the larger can stand night watch—though not enough to repel invaders, they can roughly warn off petty thieves;
translations.idiomatic: The older boys might guard my gate; they will not stop an army but may scare a thief;

sentences.zh: 小者未堪大使，為可使耘鉏穢草，驅護鳥雀。

translations.literal: the smaller are not fit for great missions, yet can weed foul grass and drive off birds.
translations.idiomatic: the younger can weed the garden and shoo birds.

sentences.zh: 休侯人則一事廢，一日獵則眾業散，不親自經營則功不攝；

translations.literal: If the field-watchers rest one day, one task fails; if one day is given to hunt, many trades scatter; if the lord does not manage himself, work is not gathered;
translations.idiomatic: Lose one farmhand and a chore stalls; lose a hunt-day and a dozen trades scatter;

sentences.zh: 常自躬親，不委下吏而已。
