translations.literal: I always manage in person and do not leave it to subordinate clerks only."
translations.idiomatic: I must do these tasks myself."

sentences.zh: 陛下聖仁，恩詔三至，士子給國，長不複發。

translations.literal: Your Majesty is sage and humane; thrice your grace has descended; gentlemen given to the state are not to be levied again.
translations.idiomatic: Your edict thrice promised: boys pledged to the state would not be called again.

sentences.zh: 明詔之下，有若皦日，保金石之恩，必明神之信，畫然自固，如天如地。

translations.literal: Under the bright edict it was like the blazing sun; I trusted favor hard as metal and stone, sure as the bright spirits—firm as heaven and earth.
translations.idiomatic: That order shone like noon; I trusted it like iron, like oath before the gods.

sentences.zh: 定習業者並復見送，晻若晝晦，悵然失圖。

translations.literal: Yet those fixed in training were again summoned for delivery—dark as noon turned dusk; I was lost and without plan.
translations.idiomatic: Now you take even my trainees—day turned to night; I am lost.

sentences.zh: 伏以為陛下既爵臣百寮之右，居藩國之任，為置卿士，屋名為宮，冢名為陵，不使其危居獨立，無異於凡庶。

translations.literal: I humbly suppose that since Your Majesty has ranked your servant above the hundred officials and set him in a princely charge, appointed ministers for him, called his house a palace and his tomb a hill, you would not let him stand in peril alone no different from common folk.
translations.idiomatic: You made me a prince, gave me ministers, called my house a palace—surely you did not mean to leave me as poor as any peasant.

sentences.zh: 若柏成欣於野耕，子仲樂於灌園；

translations.literal: If like Bo Cheng you rejoice in plowing the wilds, or Zizhong take joy in watering gardens;
translations.idiomatic: If I were Bo Cheng at the plow or Zizhong at the well—

sentences.zh: 蓬戶茅牖，原憲之宅也；

translations.literal: wicker gate and thatch window was Yuan Xian’s dwelling;
translations.idiomatic: a wattle gate was good enough for Yuan Xian;

sentences.zh: 陋巷簞瓢，顏子之居也：臣才不見效用，常慨然執斯志焉。

translations.literal: narrow lane, basket and gourd, was Yan Hui’s abode: your servant’s talent has not been put to use, yet I have often held this resolve with a sigh.
translations.idiomatic: a narrow lane enough for Yan Hui—I have no use for rank, yet I sigh toward such simplicity.

sentences.zh: 若陛下聽臣悉還部曲，罷官屬，省監官，使解璽釋紱，追柏成、子仲之業，營顏淵、原憲之事，居子臧之廬，宅延陵之室。

translations.literal: If Your Majesty would hear me return all retainers, dismiss office-holders, reduce overseers, let me undo seal and cord, and pursue Bo Cheng and Zizhong’s calling, take up Yan Yuan and Yuan Xian’s affairs, dwell in Zang’s hut, house myself in Yanling’s chamber—
translations.idiomatic: Strip me of guards, seal, and stewards; let me live like Yan Hui in a lane—

sentences.zh: 如此，雖進無成功，退有可守，身死之日，猶松、喬也。

translations.literal: if so, though advancing without success, in retreat there is something to hold; on the day of death I may still compare to Pine and Qiao."
translations.idiomatic: then failure in office would still leave me honor—I could die like an immortal hermit."

sentences.zh: 然伏度國朝終未肯聽臣之若是，固當羈絆於世繩，維繫於祿位，懷屑屑之小憂，執無已之百念，安得蕩然肆志，逍遙於宇宙之外哉？

translations.literal: Yet I humbly measure that the court will never hear me in this; I must be bound by worldly cords, tied to salary and rank, hug petty cares without end, grasp a hundred thoughts without cease—how can I roam free beyond the universe?
translations.idiomatic: Yet you will never free me—I stay tied to stipend and fret, never walking the void.

sentences.zh: 此願未從，陛下必欲崇親親，篤骨肉，潤白骨而榮枯木者，惟遂仁德以副前恩詔。

translations.literal: This wish not followed—if Your Majesty must exalt loving kin, thicken flesh and bone, moisten white bones and honor withered wood—then only follow humane virtue to match your former gracious edicts."
translations.idiomatic: If you will not loose my bonds, then honor your old mercy and spare my last boys."

sentences.zh: 』皆遂還之。〉

translations.literal: All were thereupon returned.〉
translations.idiomatic: They sent the boys back.〉

sentences.zh: 其年冬，詔諸王朝六年正月。

translations.literal: That winter an edict ordered the princes to attend court in the first month of the sixth year.
translations.idiomatic: That winter he summoned all princes to Luoyang for New Year of 232.

sentences.zh: 子志嗣，徙封濟北王。

translations.literal: His son Zhi succeeded and was transferred in enfeoffment to King of Jibei.
translations.idiomatic: His son Cao Zhi inherited the title and was moved to Jibei.

sentences.zh: 景初中詔曰：『陳思王昔雖有過失，既克己慎行，以補前闕，且自少至終，篇籍不離於手，誠難能也。

translations.literal: In the Jingchu period an edict stated: "Prince Si of Chen in the past though he had faults, has restrained himself and walked carefully to amend prior lapses; moreover from youth to end his writings never left his hand—truly it is hard to match."
translations.idiomatic: Under Jingchu an edict ran: “Cao Zhi sinned once, then mended his ways; brush never left his hand—a rare man.”

sentences.zh: 其收黃初中諸奏植罪狀，公卿已下議尚書、秘書、中書三府、大鴻臚者皆削除之。

translations.literal: Collect all memorials from the Huangchu period accusing Zhi of crimes, and the discussions from dukes and ministers down through the three offices of the Secretariat and the Grand Herald—let all be struck out.
translations.idiomatic: He ordered every Huangchu charge-sheet against Zhi burned from the archives.

sentences.zh: 撰錄植前後所著賦頌詩銘雜論凡百餘篇，副藏內外。

translations.literal: Compile and record Zhi’s fu, eulogies, poems, inscriptions, and assorted treatises in all more than a hundred pieces, with copies deposited inside and out.
translations.idiomatic: Zhi’s hundred-odd works were copied into palace and public stores.

sentences.zh: 』志累增邑，並前九百九十戶。

translations.literal: Zhi (Cao Zhi’s son) repeatedly had his fief increased; together with prior grants it came to nine hundred ninety households."
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhi’s heir saw his appanage raised in steps to nine hundred ninety households in all."

sentences.zh: 〈志別傳曰：志字允恭，好學有才行。

translations.literal: 〈The separate biography of Zhi (Cao Zhi) states: Zhi, courtesy name Yungong, loved learning and had conduct and ability.〉
translations.idiomatic: 〈Cao Zhi the son: courtesy Yungong, a learned and capable man.〉

sentences.zh: 晉武帝為中撫軍，迎常道鄉公於鄴，志夜與帝相見，帝與語，從暮至旦，甚器之。

translations.literal: When Jin Wu served as Central Army Protector and welcomed the Duke of Changdao Village at Ye, Zhi met the emperor by night; the emperor spoke with him from dusk to dawn and thought very highly of him.
translations.idiomatic: When Sima Yan met Cao Zhi at Ye they talked from dusk till dawn; he thought highly of him.

sentences.zh: 及受禪，改封鄄城公。

translations.literal: When he received the abdication, he changed the enfeoffment to Duke of Juancheng.
translations.idiomatic: At his accession he made Zhi Duke of Juancheng.

sentences.zh: 發詔以志為樂平太守，歷章武、趙郡，遷散騎常侍、國子博士，後轉博士祭酒。

translations.literal: He issued an edict appointing Zhi governor of Leping, then Zhangwu and Zhao commanderies, promoted him to Palace Attendant and Erudite of the Imperial Academy, later transferred to Libationer of the Academy.
translations.idiomatic: He sent Zhi through Leping, Zhangwu, and Zhao to Palace Attendant, academy erudite, then chancellor of students.

sentences.zh: 及齊王攸當之藩，下禮官議崇錫之典，志嘆曰：『安有如此之才，如此之親，而不得樹本助化，而遠出海隅者乎？

translations.literal: When Prince You of Qi was to go to his fief, the ritual officials were ordered to debate the honors of investiture; Zhi sighed, saying, "How can there be such talent, such kinship, yet not plant roots to aid transformation, and instead be sent far to the sea’s edge?"
translations.idiomatic: When Sima You was packed off to his fief, Zhi cried: “So much wit, so close a brother—yet you send him to the coast?”

sentences.zh: 』乃建議以諫，辭旨甚切。

translations.literal: Thereupon he set forth a remonstrance; the wording was very cutting.
translations.idiomatic: He drafted a blunt memorial against it.

sentences.zh: 帝大怒，免志官。

translations.literal: The emperor was greatly angered and dismissed Zhi from office.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor sacked him in a rage.

sentences.zh: 後復為散騎常侍。

translations.literal: Later he again became Palace Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Later he was again Palace Attendant.

sentences.zh: 志遭母憂，居喪盡哀，因得疾病，喜怒失常，太康九年卒，謚曰定公。〉

translations.literal: Zhi met his mother’s bereavement, observed mourning with full grief, thereby fell ill, joy and anger lost balance, died in the ninth year of Taikang, posthumous name Duke Ding.〉
translations.idiomatic: He mourned his mother to illness, lost his temper, and died in 288—posthumously Duke Ding.〉

sentences.zh: 蕭懷王曹熊

translations.literal: Prince Xiaohuai, Cao Xiong.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Xiong, Prince Xiaohuai.

sentences.zh: 蕭懷王熊，早薨。

translations.literal: Prince Xiaohuai Xiong died young.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Xiong, Prince Xiaohuai, died in childhood.

sentences.zh: 黃初二年追封謚蕭懷公。

translations.literal: In the second year of Huangchu he was posthumously enfeoffed and titled Duke Xiaohuai of Xiao.
translations.idiomatic: In 221 he was posthumously named Duke Xiaohuai of Xiao.

sentences.zh: 太和三年，又追封爵為王。

translations.literal: In the third year of Taihe his noble rank was again posthumously raised to king.
translations.idiomatic: In 229 his posthumous rank was raised to prince.

sentences.zh: 青龍二年，子哀王炳嗣，食邑二千五百戶。

translations.literal: In the second year of Qinglong, his son, Prince Ai Bing, succeeded, with food-revenue of two thousand five hundred households.
translations.idiomatic: In 234 his son Cao Bing inherited, with twenty-five hundred households.

sentences.zh: 六年薨，無子，國除。

translations.literal: In the sixth year he died without son; the state was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: He died in 238 without heir; the fief was struck out.

sentences.zh: 評曰：任城武藝壯猛，有將領之氣。

translations.literal: The appraiser states: Rencheng was fierce and mighty in martial arts, bearing the air of a commander.
translations.idiomatic: The historian’s verdict: Cao Zhang combined raw strength and martial dash—he was born to lead armies.

sentences.zh: 陳思文才富艷，足以自通後葉，然不能克讓遠防，終致攜隙。

translations.literal: Prince Si of Chen’s literary talent was rich and brilliant, enough to communicate himself to later ages, yet he could not restrain himself in yielding nor take long precautions, and in the end brought about estrangement.
translations.idiomatic: Cao Zhi’s genius was lush enough to speak across the centuries, yet he could not yield nor look far ahead—and so he came to grief with his kin.

sentences.zh: 傳曰『楚則失之矣。

translations.literal: The tradition says, “Chu then lost it.
translations.idiomatic: The old gloss runs: “Chu missed the mark—

sentences.zh: 而齊亦未為得也』，其此之謂歟！

translations.literal: Yet Qi too cannot be called having got it right”—is this not what is meant!
translations.idiomatic: yet Qi hardly did better”—surely that saying fits this case!

sentences.zh: 〈魚豢曰：諺言『貧不學儉，卑不學恭』，非人性分也，勢使然耳。

translations.literal: 〈Yu Huan says: The proverb states, “The poor do not learn thrift from study; the lowly do not learn respect from study”—this is not human nature’s allotment; circumstance makes it so.
translations.idiomatic: 〈Yu Huan: “Poverty teaches thrift without lessons; low rank teaches deference without lessons”—not fate, but force of circumstance.

sentences.zh: 此實然之勢，信不虛矣。

translations.literal: This is indeed the force of circumstance; truly it is not empty.
translations.idiomatic: That is how power shapes men—no empty word.

sentences.zh: 假令太祖防遏植等，在於疇昔，此賢之心，何緣有窺望乎？

translations.literal: Suppose the Grand Progenitor had checked Zhi and the others in the past—how could these worthy men’s hearts have had any peering ambition?
translations.idiomatic: Had Cao Cao curbed Zhi early, would loyal hearts ever have dreamed of the throne?

sentences.zh: 彰之挾恨，尚無所至。

translations.literal: Zhang’s harbored resentment still did not reach that far.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang’s bitterness never went that far.

sentences.zh: 至於植者，豈能興難？

translations.literal: As for Zhi—how could he have raised rebellion?
translations.idiomatic: As for Zhi—could he ever have raised a revolt?

sentences.zh: 乃令楊脩以倚註遇害，丁儀以希意族滅，哀夫！

translations.literal: Yet it led to Yang Xiu’s being killed for leaning and annotating, Ding Yi’s clan extinction for currying intent—alas!
translations.idiomatic: Yet Yang Xiu died for taking Zhi’s part, Ding Yi’s whole house perished for flattery—how pitiful!

sentences.zh: 餘每覽植之華採，思若有神。

translations.literal: Whenever I peruse Zhi’s splendid brilliance, my thought is as if there were a spirit.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I read Zhi’s verse, I feel something almost daemonic in it.

sentences.zh: 以此推之，太祖之動心，亦良有以也。〉

translations.literal: Pushing from this, the Grand Progenitor’s stirred heart also had good reason.〉
translations.idiomatic: Small wonder Cao Cao’s heart wavered when faced with such a gift.〉
